Your AI Agent Doesn't Belong Inside an HTTP Request

📅 Nov 01, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

A user sends a message to your AI application.

Your server receives:

POST /api/chat

So you do what seems natural:

app.post('/api/chat', async (c) => { const result = await runAgent(await c.req.json()); return c.json(result); });

It works.

Then your Agent gets smarter. Instead of one LLM call, it starts doing this:

User │ ▼ Agent │ ├── LLM call ├── search ├── database query ├── tool call ├── another LLM call ├── file generation └── final LLM call

The request that used to take 5 seconds now takes 30 seconds, then 2 minutes, then 10.

The HTTP request is still there, but the HTTP connection is a poor place to represent the lifetime of an Agent.

The Problem With Connection-Bound Agents

Consider this architecture:

Browser │ │ POST /api/agent ▼ Node.js │ │ await ▼ Agent │ ├── LLM ├── Tool ├── LLM ├── Tool └── LLM │ ▼ HTTP response

The entire Agent run is coupled to one HTTP request. That raises an uncomfortable question:

What happens when the browser disconnects?

A server can detect a client disconnect through the request's AbortSignal and combine it with a server timeout:

const signal = AbortSignal.any([ timeoutSignal, c.req.raw.signal, ]);

Then it passes the signal into the upstream LLM request:

await fetch(LLM_URL, { signal });

For a normal streaming chat response, this is what you want. If the user closes the tab halfway through, continuing to generate is wasteful.

An Agent is different.

A Chat Response Is Not an Agent Run

Compare two operations.

Operation A: Generate an answer

User │ ▼ POST /chat │ ▼ LLM │ ▼ stream response

The operation exists to serve the current connection. If the user leaves, cancelling the generation makes sense.

Operation B: Run an Agent

User │ ▼ POST /agents │ ▼ Agent │ ├── search web ├── inspect documents ├── call tools ├── write files ├── run code └── generate final report

This is no longer a response. It is a task, and tasks have their own lifecycle.

The Browser Is Not the Owner of the Task

Tying an Agent to the connection says:

"This Agent exists as long as this browser connection exists."

What the user actually asked is:

"Perform this task for me."

Those are different lifetimes. The browser connection might last 10 seconds while the task takes 10 minutes:

Browser connection │ │ short-lived ▼ HTTP request Agent task │ │ long-lived ▼ Task lifecycle

This is the same boundary the previous article ran into with cancellation. A client disconnect does not prove the server cancelled the work, and a server cancellation does not prove the provider stopped inference. Each of those is a separate fact.

Now take it one step further. Suppose the Agent has already searched, queried the database, and generated a file, and then the user closes the browser. If the request was:

"Research these 20 documents and generate a report."

you probably don't want:

Browser closed ↓ Agent killed ↓ report lost

The user didn't cancel the task. They closed the UI.

The Task Gets Its Own Identity

Instead of running the Agent inside the request, the request creates a task and returns:

POST /api/agents { "taskId": "task_01J..." }

The HTTP request is finished. The Agent continues on its own:

HTTP request │ ▼ create task ──────────► task_123 │ │ ▼ ▼ HTTP response Agent │ ├── LLM ├── Tool └── LLM

The task ID is an identity for the work itself:

Before: HTTP request = work After: task ID = work

That lets you store the task and make the database, not the connection, the source of truth:

type AgentTask = { id: string; status: 'queued' | 'running' | 'completed' | 'failed' | 'cancelled'; createdAt: Date; startedAt?: Date; completedAt?: Date; error?: string; };

The browser stops owning the Agent. It owns a subscription to the Agent's progress:

POST /api/agents → task_123 GET /api/agents/task_123 → current status GET /api/agents/task_123/events → live progress

A client can connect, disconnect, and reconnect. The task doesn't care.

Reconnection becomes ordinary. The user starts an Agent at 12:00 and the browser crashes at 12:01. At 12:05 the user reopens the app, and the frontend asks:

GET /api/agents/task_123 { "id": "task_123", "status": "completed" }

Nothing required the original TCP connection to survive five minutes.

The code for this article is a runnable demo: aiengineering-book/agent-task-demo. It runs the same simulated Agent bound to a request and as a task, drops the connection partway through, cancels at different points, evicts a subscriber that stops reading, and checks what survives each time.

Streaming Becomes a Subscription

This doesn't mean you should stop streaming. Streaming is still the right way to deliver progress. What changes is what the stream represents:

Streaming becomes a view of a task, not the task itself.

The task emits events:

task.started tool.started tool.completed llm.started llm.delta llm.completed task.completed

and any number of browsers can render them as they arrive:

Agent task │ │ events ▼ ┌───────────────┐ │ Event stream │ └───────┬───────┘ │ ┌───────┴────────┐ ▼ ▼ Browser A Browser B

An SSE response is a subscription to task_123. It is not where the Agent lives:

Task lifecycle ───────────────────────────────────────► Agent running Browser A ───────────────X Browser B ────────────────►

The subscription can disappear without destroying the work. The LLM stream itself moves one level down: it feeds the task's event stream instead of feeding the HTTP response directly.

Once the task is independent of HTTP, the server no longer has to execute it either. The API accepts the request, validates input, creates the task, and hands it to a worker. The worker owns execution.

Disconnect and Cancel Are Different Operations

With a task, "the browser went away" and "the user wants this stopped" stop being the same event.

Disconnect

Browser X │ ▼ subscription ended Agent continues

Cancel

POST /api/agents/task_123/cancel

Now the user has said explicitly: stop this task. That is a different semantic, and it lets you keep several policies side by side:

Event What happens User disconnects The subscription ends. The Agent continues. User presses Stop The task is cancelled. Task runs longer than its limit (for example 30 minutes) The task is cancelled. Server shuts down (SIGTERM) Task state is persisted. The task resumes later.

These are four different events. Collapsing them into one AbortSignal hides the difference between them.

A cancel request also needs a precise answer. "Cancelled" can mean different things depending on how far the work had got, and a status that hides the difference is misleading:

Outcome Meaning Client detached The subscription ended. Nothing was cancelled. Queued work cancelled The task had not started. Nothing ran. Tool call cancelled A running step stopped before it finished. Side effect already committed A step finished before the cancel arrived and cannot be undone.

Return which of these happened. In the demo, the cancel endpoint answers step_cancelled or side_effect_committed. Give the task an ID that appears in every log line across the browser, the API, the worker, and the provider call, so the sequence can be reconstructed afterwards.

What You Take On

Decoupling the task from the connection doesn't make the hard parts disappear. It moves them somewhere you have to design for.

  • Dead subscribers. A subscription that goes quiet without a clean close can leave a stale connection holding resources, and proxies and load balancers close idle connections. Send periodic heartbeats on the event stream so a healthy connection stays open. Heartbeats do not help you spot a dead one. On a one-way stream the server never hears back, and its own writes keep the socket looking active, so an idle timer cannot tell a quiet client from a gone one. What gives a stuck reader away is backpressure: its socket stops draining, writes back up, and the server can drop that subscription after a short drain timeout. The demo does exactly that, and the task keeps running.
  • Task state. A task moves through queued, running, and one of completed, failed, cancelled. The task decides these states, not the HTTP connection.
  • Worker failure. If a worker crashes mid-task, the task is still running in the database. Something has to notice that the worker disappeared, and then retry, resume, or mark the task failed.
  • Durable steps. An Agent that searches, writes a file, calls an API, updates a database, and sends an email can crash after step four. Restarting blindly repeats work, so the task has to record which steps are done.
  • Idempotency. If the Agent sends an email and crashes before recording that it did, a retry sends it twice. Steps with side effects need idempotency keys or a record of completion.
  • Tools that outlive the abort. If the model has emitted a tool call, cancelling the LLM stream does nothing for the work that tool already started. Tools need to check the task's cancellation signal themselves, and be safe to run twice.

None of these are specific to AI. They are the standard problems of background work, and Agents run into them early because a single Agent run is already many asynchronous steps. Each deserves more space than this article can give it.

When to Bind Work to HTTP

Not every operation needs a task. For plain chat:

request ↓ LLM ↓ stream ↓ response

binding the work to the connection is reasonable, and cancelling when the user leaves is often exactly right.

The previous article measured one provider on one day: DeepSeek, streaming chat requests, aborted at two points. Billing followed the abort point and stayed far below the cost of running each request to its token limit. For plain chat in that test, cancel-on-disconnect was cheap and effective. That is one provider, not a general statement, but it points to where the real reason to decouple Agents lies. It isn't cost. It is that an Agent run has side effects and results the user still wants after the tab is gone.

Ask one question:

If the user closes the browser, should the work still exist?

If the answer is no, use connection cancellation. If the answer is yes, create a task and return its ID.

You can sort most AI operations into three patterns:

Pattern Shape Examples Disconnect Request-bound HTTP → LLM → HTTP response chat completion, short transformations, simple streaming Can cancel the work Persisted HTTP → create work → storage → background processing document indexing, file processing, generation written to history Should not cancel the work Resumable Agent task HTTP → task ID → worker (LLM, tools, checkpoints, state) research agents, coding agents, multi-step workflows The UI is just a client of the task

The rule isn't "never run an Agent inside an HTTP request". It is:

Don't bind the lifetime of durable work to the lifetime of an ephemeral connection.

Final Takeaway

The first generation of AI applications looked like this:

HTTP request → LLM → HTTP response

That is fine for chat. Agents introduce something different:

HTTP request → create task → Agent → many asynchronous operations → durable result

Once work can outlive the browser connection, the connection should no longer own it:

┌──────────────────┐ │ Connection │ │ │ │ short-lived │ │ disposable │ │ reconnectable │ └────────┬─────────┘ │ │ subscribes to ▼ ┌──────────────────┐ │ Task │ │ │ │ durable │ │ cancellable │ │ resumable │ └────────┬─────────┘ │ ▼ ┌──────────────────┐ │ Agent Runtime │ │ │ │ LLMs │ │ Tools │ │ State │ │ Checkpoints │ └──────────────────┘

The browser connection is ephemeral. The Agent task is the thing that matters.

The rule

If the work should survive the connection, don't make the connection own the work.

Further Reading

This is the third article in a series about what happens when a user closes the tab. Part 1 covers how a disconnect reaches your server and how to propagate it upstream with AbortSignal. Part 2 measures whether aborting the request actually stops the provider.

The demo code is in aiengineering-book/agent-task-demo.

The server-side patterns this article builds on, including the difference between non-persisted chat work, persisted work, and long-running Agent tasks, are covered in Chapter 3 of 《AI Engineering with TypeScript — A Comprehensive Guide to Building AI Agents》 at Leanpub. The book's companion code is at github.com/aiengineering-book/code.

Overview: Stocks Under $5

Stocks that trade under $5 are considered cheap stocks. But unlike stocks under $10 or stocks under $20, stocks under $5 are in a separate category. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) considers stocks that trade under $5 to be penny stocks. Yes, these are often the best cheap stock to buy even if they’re called “penny stocks”. When you do your research, a term like penny stock shouldn’t scare you. Market insights often indicate that these stocks can gain and are even good for swing trading.

True, an investment advisor might not zero in on these stocks first, but you might consider adding these assets to your portfolio so that you have some room for growth. However, room for growth requires patience. Impatient investors may want to look into swing trading or day trading options, which allows them to maximize their profits, enhance their portfolios and plan for the future.

For example, Costco (NASDAQ: COST) is a discount retailer that hosts customers in large warehouses. Even so, it’s stock regularly trades for several hundred dollars per share and the company is one of the largest retailers in the world. While this is an extreme example, it shows that terminology only paints a small part of the picture. You must monitor these assers, choose a trading strategy that works for today—not “whenever”. Determine when you will exit the position. Decide if you can invest for value in these stocks, how much you’re willing to spend and if that budget will change based on what you learn about the asset.

How Much Money Can You Make From Stocks?

Let’s say you invest $300 for 100 shares of a stock trading at $3. If that stock price goes up by only $3, you will have made 100% in profit, or $300. Huge payoffs for little upfront capital is what makes cheap stocks an attractive investment. At the same time, you don’t want to assume that these investments will pan out every time. Spend money you are prepared to lose because it’s difficult to know where a stock will move, especially if you’re investing with savings or retirement funds.

However, you must understand that cheap stocks are very close to 0 or being delisted. This does not mean that all cheap stocks will lose value, but a stock that isn’t all that expensive could easily plummet overnight, leaving with tough decisions to make. This is why investment management takes quite a lot of patience and information—in fact, the help of a professional or informational platform like Benzinga can go a long way.

A strategy for spotting potential in stocks under $5 is to look out for undervalued companies. Companies that have suffered a crisis might see stock prices dip into the low single digits. Executive mismanagement, high debt, pricing pressures and increased competition are some of the factors that spook stockholders and send a company’s stock sinking seemingly without warning. But, those that are monitoring the markets carefully will see these issues come about through small items in the news cycle until they become too big too ignore.

But the company might be able to turn things around. Management can change, debt can be restructured or the market could shift in the company’s favor. Everyone loves a comeback — especially if you’ve scooped up that stock for a bargain. Bargains can turn into profits, but it depends on how long they last. You must carefully monitor your portfolio to ensure certain bargains you thought would soar aren’t tanking.

Another way to spot a potential winner is by looking at companies that have major growth potential. A stock could trade under $5 because the company is small. But that small company could also be rapidly growing. Their market capitalization may be low today, but that can change quickly, especially given recent market volatility.

Features to Look for

Here are some things you may want to consider as you gather stocks under $5 into your basket:

  • Earnings per share: A great way to get a sense of a company’s profitability is by looking at its earnings per share (EPS). You can find a company’s EPS by subtracting the preferred dividends from net income and then dividing the difference by outstanding stockholder shares. If you spot a stock with EPS that has been growing, it can signal growth potential. 
  • Trading volume: A stock’s trading volume will tell you how many shares are traded during the day. If the trading volume isn’t high enough, you may not be able to sell your position. Stocks that have a trading volume of at least 1 million tend to be safer. Keeping an eye on the trading volume will also help you spot stocks that may be on the uptick. 
  • Management: A management team that is set on turning the company around can be the reason a stock under $5 enjoys a boost. A company’s focus on capitalizing on a growing market is another sign of potential. Look into the company’s strategic business plan to understand the mindset of management.
  • Growth potential: The question is, will you hold this stock or unload it when you believe it has reached its potential. Some people even find that stocks under $5 fit into retirement accounts because of their growth potential, and they could continue to grow because of their low pricing simply because companies that are trying to grow rapidly are incentivized to help that stock value rise over time.

Weigh The Risk

When you find a few cheap stocks to buy right now, they carry both growth potential and their fair share of risks. Even the best stocks to buy under $5 are notorious for major upswings and selloffs because they have not yet fully matured. Your risk for loss is also higher if the company hits a difficult roadblock.

It’s not unheard of for companies with shares trading under $5 to go under and leave investors with nothing. At the same time, a price change could occur at any time, turning a stock that routinely sits under $5 into a growth asset with an emerging market cap.

Avoid putting all your money into these stocks and diversify with safer assets like blue-chip stocks or bonds. The best cheap stocks to buy can be a valuable addition to your investment portfolio with your due diligence and diversification. Stocks to buy now cheap can become a lovely addition to your portfolio, so long as you return to Benzinga often to research each new security.

When you find stocks that are listed under $5, remember that they could linger or rise. Some people want to hold for the long-term, but others want to swing trade and move on. Decide what sort of investor you want to be before filling your portfolio with affordable assets.

Overview: Biotech Stocks

Biotech companies are a subsector of healthcare stocks that primarily focus on developing new drugs and treatments for medical conditions, diseases and viruses. The stock value and growth potential of a biotech firm depend on the type of diseases it treats. This might also include the research that the firm does as it supports other companies, diseases or treatments.

For instance, a biotech firm working on breast cancer treatments, which has nearly 300,000 new cases in the U.S. each year, might be more valuable than a company that is developing drugs for Ogilvie’s Syndrome, a rare disease that only affects 1%–3% of the population. 

Every new drug developed by biotech firms has to be submitted to the Food and Drug Association (FDA) for approval. Medical companies spend years developing a new drug but may fail to get it approved by the FDA. Some of these drugs will never hit the shelf of pharmaceuticals even after countless clinical trials. On the other hand, if a biotech company gets a new drug sanctioned by the FDA and the demand is high, the stock value can double or even triple overnight.

Features to Look for in Biotech Stock

  • Earnings per share: You can determine the profitability of a company by its earnings per share (EPS). It is calculated by dividing the net income of the company by the total number of its outstanding shares.
  • Price-earnings ratio: The price-earnings ratio (P/E ratio) is calculated by dividing the current stock price by its EPS. Based on the P/E ratio, you can assess if a stock is undervalued or overvalued. The lower the P/E ratio of the stock, the better an investment it is. Generally, penny stocks under $5 have the lowest P/E ratios. 
  • Medical innovation: Biotech firms can spend years conducting clinical trials to test a new drug. Keep a constant watch on any news regarding medical breakthroughs and FDA approvals to make the most of your trade.   
  • Relevancy: Apart from medical innovation, you need to invest in stocks that are relevant—and continue to remain relevant. Research specifically what these companies do, drugs they’re working on, therapies that they have created and how those ideas remain in the headlines, even if the company is rather old.

Be Patient for Better Profits

Advanced medical technology has led to longer and more fulfilling lives. An investment in biotech stocks involves longer buy-and-hold periods, but if you are patient with your trades, you can strike gold when you least expect it. Remember, the biotech industry can shift very quickly, like during the COVID-19 pandemic. Be patient, do the research and don’t be afraid to exit positions that might not work well for you. Every industry shifts at different times, and that’s why patience is so critical for investors.

              If you plan to diversify your portfolio in light of recent events, investing in gold stocks could be a good choice. Gold stocks not only track the movements of gold prices that tend to rise in uncertain times, but they also generally gain value in a rising stock market. 

              Gold stocks could serve as a hedge to stocks you hold from other economic sectors. Gold stocks can also be traded speculatively in the current economic environment. 

              Keep in mind that gold stocks can vary considerably in price and investment quality, ranging from highly-rated stocks to pink-sheet penny stocks. The best gold stocks for your portfolio will depend on your risk tolerance and financial objectives.

              Overview

              Newmont Corporation (NYSE: NEM) is the world’s largest gold mining stock. The Greenwood Village, Colorado-based company was incorporated in 1921 after being founded in 1916 by William Boyce Thompson. The company employs 24,000 people worldwide. 

              Barrick Gold Corp. (NYSE: GOLD) is one of the largest gold mining companies in the world and is based in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. The company was founded by Peter Munk and was listed as a publicly-traded company on the Toronto Stock Exchange in 1983. 

              Kirkland Lake Gold (NYSE: KL) is based in Toronto and was founded by Brian Hinchcliffe and Harry Dobson in 1994. The company began operations as Brimstone Gold Corporation, growing through key acquisitions such as Foxpoint Resources in Vancouver and Kirkland Lake in Ontario.

              Features to Look for in a Gold Stock

              • A strong balance sheet: As with stocks in general, a strong balance sheet with consistent earnings per share growth would qualify a stock for consideration. The balance sheet will also indicate the amount of cash on hand and the amount of debt outstanding. A miner needs cash flow to find more gold and to maintain the gold it holds in reserves, while more cash also generally indicates lower debt. 
              • Location of mining operations: Most investment-grade mining companies operate multiple mines in their base country, as well as in other countries where the company owns an interest in mines and mining operations. Mines operated abroad could be at risk for a number of reasons, including geopolitical concerns, although most mining companies work with the governing bodies of the countries where their mines are located. Ideally, mines located abroad should be in politically stable countries in order to mitigate geopolitical risks.  
              • Solid operating margins: In the gold mining business, the better the margins, the higher the cash flow. The margins for gold miners tend to improve as the gold price trends higher, thereby fueling further upside in the price of gold stocks. 

              Is Now the Time to Buy?

              The gold mining sector has been one of the few segments of the overall economy that managed to gain value during the COVID-19 world health crisis. The gains in gold stocks can be attributed to the surge in the price of gold, with many companies adjusting to temporary mine closings all over the world. Remember, though, that certain stocks could suffer for reasons not related to the industry. Plus, the gold industry is not perfect, and it could run into slumps from time to time.

              Buying gold stock with gold at current levels makes sense if the price of gold holds strong and may present additional opportunities if the price of gold sells off.

              Overview: Oil Stocks

              Oil companies like ExxonMobil and BP are some of the oldest and largest publicly-traded firms in the petroleum industry, but there are many more with which you must contend as they handle crude oil and a range of petroleum products.

              Despite environmental headwinds, the oil and gas industry is still a multi-trillion dollar business composed of several different subsectors and business models, despite popular assumptions about both the price of oil and the function of the industry. Oil companies are split into 3 distinct groups based on where they function in the pipeline. The 3 different groups are:

              • Upstream: Companies in the upstream subsector are involved in finding oil and pulling it out of the earth. Upstream companies search the globe for new oil reservoirs and assemble drill sites for extraction. Yes, the oil they retrieve could become fuel or some other petroleum product, but they generally make money from retrieval via drilling on an oil rig or fracking in gas field—not sales. Upstream companies often face significant financial hurdles since drilling and mining equipment is cumbersome and expensive. Occidental Petroleum (NYSE: OXY) and Whiting Petroleum (NYSE: WLL) are upstream firms that recently suffered severe debt issues.
              • Midstream: Midstream companies are transportation and storage firms. At this part of the process, the raw product needs to be treated, stored and shipped to suppliers. Companies that run pipelines or own oil tankers are often referred to as midstream since they bridge the gap between the drillers and the companies refining and selling the product to the public. For example, a midstream firm brings gas products to the gas company or oil products to the refinery, etc.
              • Downstream: Finally, we have the refiners and suppliers. Downstream companies remove imperfections from the raw product and turn it into engine oil, gasoline, heating oil, etc. Many downstream companies also have operations in the midstream sector as well, allowing them to hold the inventory they ship. In some cases, crude oil production can lead to a transportation network and retail system.

              Many of the largest oil companies like ExxonMobil are known as integrated oil producers since they have branches involved in upstream, midstream and downstream operations, meaning that their stock price can be impacted by OPEC restrictions, current events everywhere from Oklahoma to South America and the Middle East and/or the rise and decline of demand (for example, the summer travel season in America.) When buying oil companies, be sure to understand what sector of the industry they reside in. Plus, the sector of the industry where the company works changes the way they operate and adjust to market shifts. For example, a smaller downstream company might have more room to adjust to a shifting market where a larger midstream company might not. Carefully considering your options and monitoring their performance is the best way to keep your portfolio in good condition.

Almost all brokers are commission-free for stocks and ETFs now, and most require no minimums to open an account.               Features to Look for in Oil Stocks

              • Manageable debt load: Oil companies are usually burdened with large amounts of debt, especially upstream companies that require expensive equipment to operate. Excessive leverage can easily cause oil companies to falter, but debt is a way of life for oil producers, so make sure the companies you buy can manage theirs. Yes, global demand is high, but there’s no guarantee that a plentiful oil well and an assumption of demand is enough to make a profitable business.
              • Stable dividend: Oil stocks are known for their fat dividends and investors have enjoyed steady income from the industry for years. However, with oil stocks in the bargain bin and no end in sight to the headwinds pressuring the industry, dividends are on the chopping block. Energy firms like Williams Companies (NYSE: WMB) currently sport high dividends, but that does not mean those dividends will last forever. Don’t chase high dividends when the industry is facing uncertainty, especially as infrastructure changes, the energy market diversifies and global oil production can change on a dime.
              • Sufficient cash reserves: Cash is king, especially when an unrelated crisis has driven demand into the ground. The energy sector is going to see some ugliness in the next few months as cash flow dries up, so companies with extra cash to deploy will be better positioned when the crisis subsides. If these businesses want to remain in the supply chain, they need to be ready for capital expenditure projects (CAPEX), changing climate policy and regulations, etc.

              Considerations When Buying Oil Assets

              Aside from “what to look for in an oil asset”, you need to know what to consider as you invest in the broader oil industry. Be on the lookout for:

              • Geopolitical issues: The greatest risk in the petroleum industry is geopolitical unrest. Energy economics shift with the tide of protests, regime changes and more. A despot could take over an oil-producing nation, take a significant role in OPEC, increase or decrease oil product and gas production and much more. Protests can tank a cheap oil stock when a refinery is shut down, and investors could become wary when they realize current events are cutting into their bottom line.
              • Market dynamics: The market is shifting every day, and you need to be aware of what the market wants, likes and needs. If you don’t know what the market thinks, do your research with Benzinga so that you can get a better idea of what’s happening out there.
              • Health and safety: Health and safety concerns can slow down production, cause greater regulation and scrutiny and impact oil prices.
              • Environmental considerations: The world will eventually run out of oil and most nations are under pressure to diversify their energy assets, meaning that oil prices and assets could suffer, depending on how flexible and innovative they are. If these companies don’t address climate change, they could suffer in the long-term.

              Trading Oil Stocks During a Price War

              There’s no sugarcoating this — oil can be a tough investment. Prices keep fluctuate often and there’s pressure on the industry from both short-term and long-term headwinds. Renewable energy was gaining traction before the crisis hit and while cheap oil may boost demand once the world gets back to normal, it becomes a tougher and tougher industry to navigate, especially for capital intensive operations in the Upstream sector. 

              However, it’s hard to resist buying quality companies when prices reach historic lows like these. The price of crude oil won’t stay low or high forever, but you can be sure that the price of a barrel is trending up over the long term. Nation worldwide don’t want to cut into their emergency reserves, and you cannot expect a massive dividend yield all the time when the market fluctuates as it does. Oil is a finicky industry – be sure to do your homework before investing in a sector facing unprecedented uncertainty.

                Overview: Solar Stocks

                Solar power is a clean and potentially limitless energy source and many companies have attempted to harness it. Solar power isn’t a single technology, either.  Energy from the sun is turned into power through 3 different methods:

                • Photovoltaics
                • Solar heating and cooling (SHC) 
                • Concentrating solar power (CSP)

                When discussing solar energy, most people are talking about photovoltaic solar systems, which convert sunlight into energy through the semiconductors lining the inside of solar panels. Concentrating solar power and solar heating and cooling systems actually use the sun’s thermal energy to create power. CSP and SHC systems are often implemented to heat public pools or provide hot water to residences.

                Despite the potential, problems still exist when it comes to implementing solar energy systems. The sun could reliably rise and set at specific times, but weather is about as trustworthy as the Smoking Man from the X-Files. A long period of inclement weather could wreak havoc on solar energy systems and storage systems are a must for any solar energy application. Daylight hours need to count for solar systems to reach max efficiency and weather often just does not want to cooperate.

                Then there’s the cost. For the average homeowner, installing a solar energy system will cost around $14,000 to get up and running and that’s after factoring in the federal tax credit. While the long-term energy savings could make this a worthy investment, most homeowners simply don’t have $14,000 in the budget to switch to a new electricity source. Some states have offered incentives, and there are companies that finance these installations without changing the user’s energy bills, but financing requires a high credit score and pre-approval from the lender used by the installer.

                Features to Look for in Solar Stocks

                Solar energy stocks haven’t been terrific investments in the last few years. Despite advances in efficiency and promotion from governments around the world, most solar stocks languished behind the S&P 500 during the decade-long bull market. There’s little doubt that solar power will be a big part of our lives in the coming years, but how long will investors be willing to wait to see more prevalent adoption? 

                When looking for solar companies to invest in, always keep a few key features in mind.

                • Debt levels: Solar energy is expensive. Panels are expensive to make, installations are expensive to perform and storage systems are expensive to maintain. These costs will likely decline in the future as the technology continues to improve, but right now solar energy firms require extensive amounts of capital. Be sure you aren’t investing in a company with an unhealthy debt level.
                • Cash flow consistency: Additionally, solar energy companies require a ton of capital to keep operations running smoothly. Much like its peers in the oil and gas business, the equipment needed to manufacture, install and maintain solar systems is costly. Even the solar panels themselves don’t come cheap! To make sure you’re investing in the best solar stocks, keep an eye on their cash flows. Cash flow and debt often go hand-in-hand here.
                • Management that believes: If you’re in it for the money, you’re in the wrong sector. Solar energy firms have an uphill battle to climb thanks to a familiar foe — inertia. Fossil fuels remain the dominant source of global energy and replacing them would require massive infrastructure changes. The management team in a solar energy company must have the longest view in the room because adoption will be a slow and arduous process. This is not the industry for corner-cutting just to make a buck.

                Where Do Solar Stocks Fit in Your Portfolio?

                Solar energy companies are attempting to serve 2 different customer bases at once. On one hand, solar power is a terrific public good that would greatly reduce fossil fuel consumption and make for a healthier environment. On the other hand, solar power systems are expensive to build and maintain and companies in the sector are often riddled with debt. 

                When adding solar stocks to your portfolio, be sure to consider the pros and cons of both the individual companies and the industry as a whole. Just because a company is attempting to do good doesn’t mean it’s a well-run firm. Always thoroughly vet solar companies before investing and have a plan for exiting a speculative trade.

                'Mother of all editors' Emacs is 50

                📅 Nov 01, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

                No lesser authority than the MIT Technology Review says that the Emacs editor has turned 50 years old. But then, it is biased — Emacs was invented in MIT's AI lab.

                Simson Garfinkel's article is simply called EMACS turns 50, but the sub-heading explains why it matters more:

                "How the MIT AI Lab's text editor gave birth to the free software movement."

                There are multiple timelines and accounts of the origins of Emacs, and it is not a single monolithic application. The name is an abbreviation for "Editing MACroS", and the original editor for which this set of macros was developed was TECO – "Text Editor and COrrector," written by Dan Murphy in 1962. Murphy died earlier this year at the age of 83.

                The inimitable Jamie Zawinski has an encyclopedic Emacs Timeline – as he mentions at the start, his interest being that he long ago maintained a fork of GNU Emacs, originally called Lucid Emacs. It's still around, under its later name XEmacs. There are a lot of forks and re-implementations of Emacs out there, and we are not going to go into all of them, or this article would become a book – one only interesting to programmer-archeologists (to use a term coined by the late great Vernor Vinge).

                As for who originally wrote those Editing Macros, though, another history has quotations from several of the people involved: On the Origin of Emacs in 1976. (Note – some of the quotes still contain the | symbols that marked quoted text.)

                This credits Lisp boffin Guy L. Steele Jr with the original work in 1975, but in it, Steele says:

                "RMS is responsible for the names 'E' and 'EMACS'. RMS still deserves 99% or 99.9% or 99.99% or 99.999% of the credit for taking a package of TECO macros and turning it into the most powerful editor on the planet."

                RMS is of course Richard Stallman, and the page also quotes some emails from RMS on October 23 and 31, 1976. Mind you, just a few years after the event, in a 1981 talk now preserved on the GNU website, Stallman said, "I began the development of EMACS in 1974 with an improvement to TECO". Like all the best FOSS, even in its very early stages, it was a collaborative effort – but around late October 1976 is when RMS took over the bulk of the development.

                Of the many forks of Emacs over its half a century of development, some are still just about hanging on in there. When we looked up the link for XEmacs, we were surprised to see that there was a new release: XEmacs 21.5.37 "lettuce" appeared just last month. And even the forks have forks: in this case, SXEmacs, last updated in 2020.

                Most of the changes in XEmacs and SXEmacs eventually made their way back upstream to GNU Emacs, which is still in active development, although as The Register reported in 2008, RMS is no longer the primary maintainer. GNU Emacs 31.1 appeared in August.

                Cards on the metaphorical table: this vulture is not an Emacs user. We have tried. A major influence was one of the Reg FOSS desk's favorite writers, Neal Stephenson, who in 1999 published an essay called In the Beginning… Was the Command Line. (It was later republished as a rather short book, but the text is still online.) In it, he says:

                "In the GNU/Linux world there are two major text editing programs: the minimalist vi (known in some implementations as elvis) and the maximalist emacs. I use emacs, which might be thought of as a thermonuclear word processor. It was created by Richard Stallman; enough said. It is written in Lisp, which is the only computer language that is beautiful. It is colossal, and yet it only edits straight ASCII text files, which is to say, no fonts, no boldface, no underlining. In other words, the engineer-hours that, in the case of Microsoft Word, were devoted to features like mail merge, and the ability to embed feature-length motion pictures in corporate memoranda, were, in the case of emacs, focused with maniacal intensity on the deceptively simple-seeming problem of editing text. If you are a professional writer–i.e., if someone else is getting paid to worry about how your words are formatted and printed–emacs outshines all other editing software in approximately the same way that the noonday sun does the stars."

                Emacs is 50-plus-year-old software, and it shows. This is a huge and complicated program: decades ago, the joke was that EMACS stood for "Eight Megs And Constantly Swapping". It is not an easy program to learn. Despite lavish documentation and a built-in tutorial, this is software so old that its terminology predates microprocessors and the personal computer.

                Its exhaustive manual is 804 pages long, and to pick some trivial examples, its terms for parts of the screen use “frame” to mean what’s now called a window, and “window” to mean what’s now called a pane. In the section on Keys, it discusses the Control and Meta keys. That’s a slight snag: you don’t have a Meta key, and neither do the authors of Emacs. It was a key on the now almost legendarily rare Space Cadet Keyboard, of which the Deskthority keyboard wiki says:

                “It is known as the holy grail of keyboards.”

                You can buy a modern replica, the Keymacs keyboard. They are hand-made in the Czech Republic, and depending on exactly what model and specifications you want, they cost from €2,998 for the Lispsaver up to €6,878 for the A624N Space Cadet.

                In other words, you can have a keyboard with a real Meta key if you want, but it is going to cost you.

                One of the problems with these historical terms, unfamiliar to anyone who wasn’t already programming in the 1970s, is that meanings drift. In the context of Emacs, "Meta" means Alt, or Opt on Macs. However, KDE also uses the Meta key – but what the KDE documentation calls "Meta" is the Windows key – or Command on Macs. Like most Linux folks, the GNOME documentation calls it the Super key.

                Names are important. They matter. Who's right, the Emacs folks or the KDE folks? Well, neither: nobody has Meta keys any more. We have Ctrl, Alt, and Cmd/Super/Windows.

                There have been valiant efforts to modernize Emacs and bring it into line with modern UI and terminology. This vulture tried to learn Aquamacs, which modernized Emacs with a native macOS UI, but sadly it's no longer maintained.

                Another, which we enjoyed trying, is ErgoEmacs, which changes the key bindings and rearranges the UI into something much more like the IBM Common User Access arrangement, as used in Windows and most Linux desktops. However, it never really caught on and you need to know your way around Emacs to install it and configure it for your regional keyboard layout.

                So complex is it to configure Emacs that there are multiple pre-configured distributions of Emacs, such as Doom Emacs, or the minimalist Emacs Solo. We wish someone did a "CUA-Macs" config, with ErgoEmacs integrated and able to pick up your existing keyboard config.

                Come to that, the Gershwin Desktop project that we mentioned along with GhostBSD last year is in active development, and it's based around GNUstep. Maybe its developers could pick up Aquamacs, and adapt it to GNUstep.

                There is a long history of such Emacs facelifts. One instance is Borland’s Sprint word-processor, one of the selling points of which was that it could emulate the user interfaces of most of the leading MS-DOS word-processors of its day (just before they all converged on IBM CUA). Before Borland acquired it, Sprint was called The Final Word, developed by musical equipment makers Mark of the Unicorn. FinalWord was based on an Emacs clone called MINCE.

                The Great Rival

                Another well-known Emacs distribution is Spacemacs, which adapts Emacs to have a more Vi-like user interface.

                Vi is the other seminal Unix text editor, as the Stephenson quote above mentions. As this article on Origins and the Evolution of Vi & Vim notes, it too dates back to 1976. Indeed, that’s the reason we chose the year in this story: Tilde, a text editor that doesn’t work like it’s 1976. One feature of Tilde we enjoy is that it supports use of the mouse even on the Linux console – which is the headline new feature of GNU Emacs 31.1.

                Vi is very much alive and well today. GNU Emacs is based on the original source code, but Vi mainly survives as re-implementations. The recreation Stephenson mentions, Elvis, lives on today in the form of nvi.

                However, by far the best known is Vim, maintained by Bram Moolenaar until his death in 2023. In the grand FOSS forking tradition, it too has forks, including Neovim, as used in Omarchy, and more recently, the AI-free Vim Classic – a new project led by Drew DeVault, who just launched the similarly LLM-free AlpineBSD. ®

                Anthropic says helping others is core to its mission. 3 philanthropy gurus say they'll believe it when they see it.

                📅 Nov 01, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →
                Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei.

                Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg/Getty Images

                • Anthropic outlined several ways it plans to give back in its IPO filing this week.
                • They include reserved shares, cofounder pledges, donation matching, and stock incentives.
                • Philanthropy gurus said it's partly "reputation management," and how the money is used will be key.

                Anthropic's IPO filing this week contained myriad revelations about the state of the AI firm's finances, as well as an eye-opening series of claims about its commitment to helping others.

                We asked three experts in the world of philanthropy what they thought of these giving pledges. Their verdict: we'll see.

                A culture of giving?

                The company behind the AI chatbot Claude, which filed this week to go public in what could be the biggest IPO in history, laid out how it plans to give back and encourage its employees to do the same.

                Anthropic's seven cofounders said they've pledged 80% of their personal stock in the startup to charitable causes, gifts that could together be worth $80 billion.

                They also said they've earmarked 5% of Anthropic's equity for a "fund devoted to the public good," and plan to set aside another 2% for every sustained 50% rise in the company's stock price, with its IPO price as the base.

                Moreover, they said that new employees are offered a donation match, meaning that for every share they pledge to give away to good causes, Anthropic creates an additional share and matches the donation.

                Anthropic said that just over half of its employees have pledged at least some of their equity, including 70% of employees hired before May 2024, and nearly 50% of those hired after that date.

                The company noted that 25% of the former group, who were offered up to a 50% match, pledged the full amount. That figure was nearly 30% for the latter group, who were offered a 25% match.

                Anthropic also said it plans to issue Class E shares — which carry limited voting rights but have no economic value — to reward tenure and charity.

                Employees stand to receive one share for every six months they stay at the company, and one Class E share for every normal share they pledge to donate, Anthropic said.

                Anthropic didn't respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.

                'Judge us on this'

                Three philanthropy experts told Business Insider via email this week that Anthropic's giving plan is promising but represents only a first step.

                "It's admirable, and it's well-designed," said Dr. Vandana Arcot, the founder and CEO of Komselj, a philanthropic strategy firm. She noted that "building it into the compensation structure makes generosity the default, not the exception."

                Arcot said Anthropic's giving seemed to be grounded in an "ethic of accountability, not abundance."

                She pointed to CEO Dario Amodei's January essay in which he said that people who get rich from AI have a responsibility to address its economic fallout.

                Arcot also cited Anthropic's $200 million commitment this summer to fund research on preparing people for AI's economic impacts.

                She said that valuing generosity "tends to help companies attract mission-driven talent and keep it, which is a business case on top of the moral one."

                She added that "defining your giving in advance is a way of saying: judge us on this."

                But Arcot said her full evaluation of Anthropic's efforts will depend on "who sits on the decision-making body, how recipients are chosen, and what gets reported."

                Bella DeVaan, the director of the Charity Reform Initiative and deputy director of the Program on Inequality and the Common Good at the Institute for Policy Studies, said there's such "dire" wealth inequality in the US that "any efforts to center the public benefit are commendable."

                However, she said they're "no substitute for structural reform," and "giving to the public benefit shouldn't be voluntary, but should be guaranteed by our tax system."

                DeVaan also noted the charitable pledges by Anthropic's cofounders aren't legally binding and can be revoked. She said it was "concerning" to see that personal interest could trump public benefit, and added that it's "exactly why voluntary efforts alone won't be sufficient to rely on."

                Hans Peter Schmitz, a professor of nonprofit leadership at North Carolina State University, said he applauded Anthropic for promoting generosity from the top down, but it struck him as "part of an intentional effort in managing public opinion."

                He said that any positive publicity around Anthropic's giving could help differentiate it from competitors and counter bad news about AI. The nascent technology has proven contentious due to concerns about job losses, environmental damage, cybersecurity threats, and even danger to humans.

                Schmitz said Anthropic appeared to be engaging in "reputational management," as "pledges are a relatively cheap 'signal' to be viewed in a positive light."

                "Like many pledges in the past, there is also a high likelihood that it may never happen and/or a lot of the funding is channeled into a narrow set of issues, like AI safety," he said.

                Canceled port calls and cash appeals: Inside the final months of the Villa Vie Odyssey's doomed round-the-world cruise

                📅 Nov 01, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →
                The Villa Vie Odyssey was bogged down by financial trouble in its final months at sea.

                Suy SE/AFP/Getty Images

                Villa Vie Residences promised residents the world. The company's cruise ship, the Odyssey, kept circling one corner of it while finances worsened, services deteriorated, and cash calls mounted.

                "We were going in a smaller and smaller circle," said Claude Sadovsky, who joined the Odyssey when it first set sail from Belfast in September 2024. "I signed up for a world cruise, and I was in purgatory."

                By early October, Sadovsky was frustrated enough with the itinerary changes that he left the ship and returned to his home in Maui. For Starr Davis, who also joined in Belfast in 2024, it was the constant appeals for fuel money that got her to jump ship in late September. "I got so sick of all the cash calls," she said.

                For those aboard the Odyssey in its final months, the crisis grew so acute that some passengers began fundraising for crew members, residents told Business Insider.

                The financial distress culminated in the ship's abrupt halt in Cambodia on Tuesday, when passengers were given eight hours to pack up their belongings and leave. While the speed of the end came as a shock to some, residents said signs of trouble had been growing.

                "The ship was just a pressure cooker," Davis said. "You know, 'Are we going to exist?'"

                In an interview with Business Insider on Friday, Villa Vie Residences cofounder and executive chairman Mikael Petterson confirmed the company had made cost-cutting changes. "There were itinerary changes," he said. "Of course there were."

                He said the changes aboard the Odyssey — home to a "never-ending" cruise for permanent residents who bought cabins for $119,999 to $439,999 — were driven by rising fuel costs and logistical challenges.

                "When you're the first one doing something, of course you're going to make a ton of mistakes," he said.

                Petterson said roughly 88% of Villa Vie is owned by residents; the rest is owned by the founders, management team, and him. A drawback of that structure is that residents were the ones turned to when money got tight, he said: "When there's money needed, residents are naturally called upon because there's no private equity. There's no big owner."

                "When things didn't go as planned, it was a double whammy," he added.

                "That is what made Villa Vie Residences so strong, yet so weak."

                Villa Vie Residences CEO Kathy Villalba did not respond to multiple requests for comment from Business Insider. In a now-deleted apology to residents, Villalba said Villa Vie was still speaking to potential investors and "holding onto whatever hope remains." Columbia Cruise Services, Villa Vie's operational partner, did not reply to several requests for comment.

                The round-the-world route started shrinking

                Villa Vie had marketed the three-and-a-half-year voyage as a circumnavigation with more than 425 port calls across 147 countries.

                For the period between October 2024 and October 2026, its initial itinerary listed 275 ports in 69 countries and territories, or 54 sovereign nations.

                As fuel costs rose after the onset of the war with Iran and Villa Vie's financial pressures worsened, the company increasingly pared down its route: It canceled stops, slowed the ship at sea, extended stays in ports, and revisited destinations to conserve fuel and reduce operating costs.

                To see how plans changed, Business Insider compared itineraries the ship issued at four different times: its initial itinerary from October 2024; its November 2025 itinerary, which showed where it went in 2024 and 2025; one from January 2026 showing changes before the war; and an October 2026 itinerary showing this year's stops. We also reviewed messages Villalba and Petterson sent to ship residents at various points over the past three months.

                Villa Vie Odyssey passengers in Cambodia after the voyage abruptly ended.

                TANG CHHIN Sothy / AFP via Getty Images

                We found that while the ship visited 54 nations between October 2024 and October 2026, it missed some territories and called at only 198 ports — 28% fewer than originally planned. Across the two years, our comparison of the itineraries showed the ship spent nearly two fewer months at sea than initially scheduled.

                Petterson blamed the skyrocketing price of fuel: "We had no choice," he said.

                Business Insider's analysis shows the Odyssey also made itinerary changes before fuel prices rose, including in Australia and New Zealand. Residents said those appeared to be for reasons other than fuel costs.

                Planning around an ever-changing itinerary

                For some residents, the route changes turned an around-the-world voyage into one long bout of déjà vu. "We have revisited some of the same ports countless times in the last several months," Angela Nuran Gokturk, 65, said.

                Messages from Petterson and Villalba to residents demonstrated how fuel, financing, and operating costs directly shaped the ship's route.

                In a message to residents on the ship's internal messaging platform on August 1, Villalba said they would cancel a stop in Brunei and sail directly from Singapore to Nha Trang in southern Vietnam "to conserve fuel and reduce operating costs."

                On August 7, Petterson said in a memo that the ship had "aggressively reduced costs" and "redesigned itineraries to spend more time in port and consume less fuel."

                In a message on September 6, Villalba said the Odyssey would extend its stay in Ha Long, Vietnam, by one or two days, depending on "fuel availability and funding." What was meant to be a three-night stay became a 10-night layover, the revised itinerary shows.

                Residents said the route changes made it difficult to plan flights and excursions in advance. "People stopped trying to make plans because things could change literally within a few days," said Sally Stunkel, 75, who joined the ship in February.

                During the stay in Ha Long, Stunkel joined an eight-person excursion to China, but the group had already booked flights to one of the Vietnamese stops that was later cut from the itinerary. They had to buy new tickets to rejoin the ship at its revised next port.

                "We spent more money trying to chase the ship, basically, to the next port so we could then board again," she said.

                The Villa Vie Odyssey had frequent itinerary changes.

                Suy Se / AFP via Getty Images

                Singapore became a repeat stop: The ship stopped there three times between May and July, spending 16 days there in total, according to the October 20 itinerary.

                Stunkel said the one change that frustrated her most was the removal of Japan and South Korea from the itinerary. In March, the ship's public itinerary showed it was supposed to visit 19 ports in Japan and South Korea, between June 26 and August 19. In April, the itinerary was updated to instead show stops in Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, and Brunei during that period.

                Stunkel said she had bought a cabin on the cruise in part because it was scheduled to visit Japan over the summer. She said she was "extremely disappointed" by the change, adding, "Japan is my No. 1 bucket list destination."

                Onboard services like dining and internet were hit

                Some onboard services were also disrupted.

                In a memo to residents on September 10, Villalba said that because the ship had fewer residents on board and fewer staff available, dining service would be consolidated. An on-board restaurant, The Palms, would temporarily close, while breakfast and lunch would be served buffet-style. Dinner would be a combination of à la carte and buffet. Davis said residents would joke when they went to dinner that it was "slim pickings."

                Starr Davis said the final months on the ship were like a "pressure cooker."

                Starr Davis

                Internet and TV services also suffered. Two residents said the internet had become spotty and unreliable. In a September 7 memo, Villalba said she had paid an outstanding balance and that internet service was being restored.

                Paul Montoya, 68, said the internet issues especially affected digital nomads living and working on the ship. Some would have to get off at port to find a nearby hotel with internet access, he said.

                Davis said air conditioning on the ship was throttled up or down pending fuel needs, adding, "Everything was about saving fuel."

                Petterson, who did not live on the ship and said he was not closely involved in its daily operations, said the company took measures to save money that went beyond conserving fuel.

                "We were cutting back where the residents would feel it the least, and that balance sometimes was difficult," he said.

                Residents were repeatedly asked to help keep the ship moving

                Management made repeated requests for residents to help cover Villa Vie's costs.

                In April, Villa Vie offered residents an "Emergency Loan Investment Opportunity," asking them to lend tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars to the company at interest rates of 12% to 24%, according to a letter viewed by Business Insider.

                Petterson said the request netted around $2 million that helped the ship survive for a few months.

                Aerial view of the Odyssey's pool deck.

                Villa Vie Odyssey

                From April onwards, Gokturk said it was "cash call after cash call."

                Gokturk and her husband did not participate in the loan program, she said, but they contributed to later appeals, including a voluntary fuel surcharge. "It became exhausting because it was constantly, 'Hey, we need more money. We need more money. If we don't get the money, then we're not going to be able to sail,'" Gokturk said.

                The uncertainty affected the mood aboard the ship. "It became very, very difficult," she said.

                Stunkel said the cash calls felt "incessant." She continued, "We felt like they were just leaching us out of whatever we had to keep the ship moving until the last possible moment."

                Four residents said that when they heard that staff had gone unpaid, they organized a fundraiser for the crew. Montoya said residents collected about $12,000 in cash outside the ship's café and distributed it to workers in $100 bills.

                There were several times in the last couple of months when payment owed to the crew was delayed, Petterson said, including by three weeks this month. He said as of around Wednesday, the crew had been paid. An employee in the Florida office said staff had received a partial payment, and that commissions hadn't been paid in months.

                Petterson said the company had been doing everything it could to keep the ship afloat. The company had tried to make the fuel surcharge mandatory but realized the residents' contracts didn't allow for it, so it became voluntary. Some residents contributed to the surcharge, while others bought additional discounted cabins through the VIP program.

                He said he had spent July looking for outside investment. By August, the situation was dire. A potential deal with Oneil Khosa, the former CEO of Margaritaville's cruise line, fell through last week. They were out of time. Business Insider was unable to reach Khosa for comment.

                In the days since the Odyssey's journey came to a halt in Cambodia, passengers have expressed a range of emotions. Some are heartbroken that their dream retirement came crashing to an end; others are hopeful the ship will sail again. One passenger said a group of fellow passengers is working on a "Hail Mary" attempt at buying the ship.

                Petterson said the focus is on a recapitalization, adding, "Preferably we need an operational partner that can come in with a stronger hand and a bigger pocket."

                Several residents said that despite how it ended, they don't regret the experience. But Sadovsky, who left before the Odyssey came to a halt, said the voyage he thought he had bought had become unrecognizable by the time he disembarked.

                "There was no reason for me to stay because I wasn't being exposed to new places anymore," he said. "I was revisiting the same old places, and I'd rather be home."

                Additional reporting by Amanda Goh.

                I'm running the NYC marathon along with four of my BI colleagues. These are our best tips for runners and spectators alike.

                📅 Nov 01, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →
                BI's 2026 NYC marathon runners (left to right): Noah Sheidlower, Anthony DeMaio, Zak Jason, Kathleen Elkins, and Steve Russolillo

                BI

                • This post originally appeared in the BI Today newsletter.
                • You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here.

                Welcome to Marathon Sunday!

                Yours truly will be among nearly 60,000 runners taking on the five boroughs today. I've spent months training for this one — with a little help from Muse, Meta's AI agent.

                Several weeks ago, I wrote about how I had become addicted to Muse. Since then, Muse has become part of my marathon training, helping me map out long runs and shape an overall race plan. After the Staten Island half marathon last month, it even asked me, unprompted, "how'd the half go?"

                The other day, I gave Muse my bib number and asked it to track my run. I'm hoping for real-time feedback and analysis, delivered straight through my AirPods, on how my race is unfolding and how I can stay on pace to achieve my goals.

                But no AI agent can replicate the wisdom from real people.

                At Business Insider, five of us are running the NYC marathon this year. We range from a first-time marathoner (Discourse editor Zak Jason) to a true veteran in Anthony DeMaio on the sales team, who will be running his 23rd NYC marathon (and roughly his 40th overall marathon; he says he's lost count!)

                I asked them to share their best marathon advice for runners, spectators, or if you're simply trying to understand why someone would pay $330 to run 26.2 miles.

                Here's what they had to say:

                Noah Sheidlower, senior economy reporter: Live in the moment and acknowledge the spectators who came out to support. My race time last year was disappointing, but I had an absolute blast because I was high-fiving everyone and making people's days. Tap the "power up" marathon sign that little kids are holding, give a fist pump to strangers, and laugh when you see a funny sign that someone put a lot of effort into. The marathon shouldn't just be a celebration of your individual work but a community celebration honoring the greatest city on earth. Oh also, buy merch and don't feel guilty about it! I bit the bullet and got the blue jacket, and it looks so good.

                Kathleen Elkins, investing correspondent: Soak it all in! Write your name on your shirt, absorb all of the hearty cheers, give the high-fives and the smiles! When you give New Yorkers energy, they'll give it right back.

                Zak Jason, Discourse executive editor: As a first-time marathoner, I'm in no position to advise on anything — other than to trust the advice of people who have done hard things before you, because they want you to be awake to the gift of being alive. (Then again, someone also told me it's OK to pee yourself during the race.)

                Anthony DeMaio, global head of sales: Can't wait to run my 23rd NYC Marathon. The marathon is a celebration of preparation. Every early morning and every tough summer long run builds the confidence to stand on the starting line. The days you don't want to run are often the ones that matter most, discipline is choosing what you want most over what you want right now. Embrace the hard moments; they prepare you for the miles when things get tough. And remember, running is a team sport. Let people support you, and support them in return. To all my fellow runners: May the wind be at your back, the sun on your shoulders, and the crowds carry you all the way to the finish.

                And for me, my standard advice is that the first five miles can make or break a marathon. Go slower than your expected pace at the beginning. If you think you're going too slow at the onset, go even slower.

                You'll thank yourself later!

                Meta Discussed 'Whisper Strategy' to Discredit Social Media Critic Jonathan Haidt, Files Show

                📅 Nov 01, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →
                The Guardian reports: Meta staff discussed deploying a "whisper strategy" to undermine the influential US academic whose work has inspired a global social media crackdown, according to court documents. Employees at the parent group of Facebook and Instagram sought to discredit Jonathan Haidt, the social psychologist and author of The Anxious Generation, a book that helped tip the debate about online safety towards more stringent measures such as the under-16 ban in Australia. Minutes of internal meetings contained in a recent legal filing in the US showed that staff discussed how to "get the academic community to disavow Haidt". They appear in a document titled "Well-being Meeting Sound-check Notes", which refers to discussions of how Meta could "turn other academics against Haidt" and to a "whisper strategy" aimed at achieving that goal. It also mentions "debunking" his work. Minutes from a meeting on 8 March 2023 mention "Curtiss", an apparent reference to Meta's then vice-president of research, Curtiss Cobb. It states: "Curtiss's goal for this work: how do we get the academic community to disavow Haidt. Can't co-opt them, so how do we enrage them ... so the media finds him not credible." It then adds: "Not thinking about this as a loud strategy. A below-the-line campaign...." The minutes were produced before Haidt published his book in 2024 and discuss responding to a Substack post written by the academic in which he reviews "a bunch of articles". "It is not clear whether Meta acted on the ideas outlined in the minutes."

                Read more of this story at Slashdot.

                I run an 8-person startup that uses AI agents. We don't let our agents run on vibes — here's the playbook system we created

                📅 Nov 01, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →
                Rachel Woods created playbooks full of AI agents to replace additional hires at her company.

                Courtesy of Rachel Woods

                • Rachel Woods taught herself AI while studying business in college, later landing a role at Facebook.
                • She left to start her own business, which helps people integrate AI into their everyday workflows.
                • She said the company has saved itself at least 4 new hires by using AI agents and playbooks.

                This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Rachel Woods, CEO and cofounder of AMP. The following has been edited for length and clarity.

                My first official role in AI was at Facebook. I started as an intern and then joined full-time in 2018. I worked on AI research and development for the ads system that's powered by AI.

                I don't have an engineering degree or background; I studied management information systems at The University of Texas at Austin. Part of why I think I got my role at Facebook was because I spent time building my own side projects and teaching myself how to train AI models and do data analysis.

                I left Facebook in 2020 to start my own business in the wine industry, and after that company sold, I founded an AI company. I would need to double the number of people on my team if we didn't use AI playbooks.

                If you're being thoughtful about setting up your AI operations, it's no different than building a team that you can trust.

                That's something a lot of people are missing: how to actually make these systems things you can take your eyes off and not keep yourself up at night in the process.

                Business Insider wants to talk to founders of AI-powered companies with fewer than 10 workers, and employees working alongside AI agents and bots, to understand what the "Tiny Teams" era really feels like — the wins, the fears, and the human skills that stand out. Share your story by filling out this quick form.

                I've been an entrepreneur since the age of 15

                My first business was a photography business, and I was too young to even drive to meet my clients. I would always catch rides with people, and my parents hated this.

                I got into tech because in college, I was exposed to colleagues doing data analytics and working with coding and AI at summer internships. That led me to look online and try to take related classes, and I started to see that if you break a business problem into small enough pieces, you can get AI to handle parts of it: predicting, sorting, generating.

                Later, when I was applying to Facebook, I used AI and data analysis to build a report of coffee shops in Austin that were less likely to be too busy for me to study at. I think that project helped me land my role.

                After I left Facebook, I started a wine business called Vinebase in 2020; we built a tech platform that used AI to help winemakers sell their wine online and manage the digital side of their business.

                Because this was before AI became more mainstream, we didn't market it as AI. We called it our "auto magic" system. I think that if we had said it was AI, it could've been a turnoff for our customers. Vinebase was acquired by Corksy in fall 2022.

                I use my playbooks and AI agents to replace additional staff

                My sister and I started AMP, originally called The AI Exchange, before ChatGPT was released in November 2022, because I was using AI in Vinebase and saw how the technology was progressing. ChatGPT came out about a month later and started really accelerating the AI timeline, so we went all in.

                We have four full-time employees and four part-time contractors right now, but we'd need double if we weren't running as much as we are on AI. Given the company's current size, we'd need at least four to five additional people, including a sales and marketing manager, customer support specialist, executive assistant, and operations coordinator.

                The way we structure these systems is based on something we call playbooking. Every department in the company has its own system. Each system is a collection of playbooks with AI agents that can run independently or together.

                How we build our AI playbooks

                To build an AI playbook, pick one piece of work you do over and over, and write down what starts it, what goes into the task, and what should come out at the end. Next, write the steps the way you'd train a new hire: each step, the decisions in it, and what "good" looks like.

                Start running it with AI, and while you watch, compare the result to how you would've done it. Then, fix the playbook, not the output, until you trust it to run without you.

                I always think through how I want a playbook to work and outline it by hand. Whenever you're making an AI playbook, you want to own the thinking and the logic. Otherwise, you can fall into the trap of including something that you don't really understand, and then you're not going to be able to trust that system anyway.

                We have an AI agent running our sales playbook to review customer calls and ensure they meet our standards, rather than having a sales manager review them manually. Also, instead of sales team members needing to ask their manager questions, they just ask the playbook, which then pulls the answers from our guide for that team.

                There are two types of AI costs we have in the business. The first is the subscriptions to Claude and ChatGPT for every person on the team. The other is because the majority of our operations are these AI playbooks that are running in the background without us being the ones starting or triggering it. In September, we spent $8,510 on Claude Code to run our playbooks in the background, which is billed by usage and is separate from the team's monthly Claude and ChatGPT subscription costs.

                Own the playbook, rent the tech

                We say "own the playbook, rent the tech," which means that if you are creating really good playbooks for your AI to follow, it actually doesn't matter which tool you're running it in.

                Right now, we have a setup that's running with Claude Code in the background. But I could run all of these playbooks in ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, or Microsoft Copilot.

                We try to avoid a lot of the risks that people are concerned about with AI going rogue by creating these detailed outlines. We don't just want the agents to run on vibes. There still needs to be a person to decide and design how the work gets done; AI just speeds up everything else. That's the job security we have in this AI era.

                Start small, and get everyone involved

                A few of us on the team who are more advanced with AI own the bigger, team-wide playbooks that the business depends on, but everyone playbooks their own personal workflow, and then we use that as the testing ground to graduate things into becoming more part of official systems.

                My advice would be to just start with something small and really easy, because once you get your first win and see how AI can do that repetitive work for you, it's kind of like a snowball.

                Do you have a story to share about using AI to run your small team? Contact this editor, Agnes Applegate, at aapplegate@businessinsider.com.
