                Apollo is sharing its private-equity playbook with nonprofits

                📅 Nov 01, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →
                The Apollo Global Management LLC office.

                Bloomberg/Getty Images

                • Apollo Global Management gives portfolio companies operational guidance and leadership training.
                • It also provides funding and operational support to 28 nonprofits, including a biennial training summit.
                • The summit included discussions about the labor market and advice on making high-stakes decisions.

                Keeping up with AI and an uneven labor market is challenging enough for corporate leaders. For nonprofit executives working with tighter budgets and leaner teams, it can be extra daunting.

                "It's tricky for everyone right now, but for those guys, it's actually very tricky," Scott Kleinman, co-president of Apollo Asset Management and chair of the Apollo Opportunity Foundation Board.

                The foundation is addressing the challenges nonprofits face by providing 28 organizations with a version of the playbook Apollo uses with its over 190 portfolio companies, which include Yahoo Inc. and Shutterfly.

                That includes access to experts, leadership training, and a built-in network. The foundation also provides funding based on factors such as the organization's budget size and impact metrics. Apollo has so far provided over $13 million to grantees and committed to $100 million in funding over the next decade.

                The foundation, which launched in 2022, offered Business Insider an exclusive look at its biennial summit in October, where grantee leaders mingled with Apollo executives and sat in on panels led by subject-matter experts.

                Applying its portfolio playbook

                Kleinman said the foundation provides the same type of support it provides its portfolio companies, including operational guidance, data and digital transformation, talent management, and recruitment.

                "That is the crux of our foundation. Of course, it involves capital." Kleinman said, adding that the "real-value add" is the deal team.

                Each nonprofit is paired with a deal team of five to 10 employees from Apollo or Athene, which merged with Apollo and provides retirement services. Employees build relationships with the grantees to perform pro-bono projects, source board opportunities, and provide strategic advice.

                The foundation also holds monthly virtual training sessions to discuss topics like AI, leadership transitions, culture, real estate, fundraising, and succession planning.

                Beyond the funding

                At the October leadership summit, Apollo's chief economist Torsten Sløk discussed the labor market and how organizations can adapt to it, while the firm's chief financial officer talked about the factors nonprofits should consider when growing their organizations. The summit also included working sessions for grantees and their Apollo deal teams.

                The support Apollo offers grantees can be anything from fundraising skill-building to succession planning, said Lauren Coape-Arnold, Apollo Global Management's global head of citizenship and executive director of the Apollo Opportunity Foundation.

                She said the partnership starts with reorganizing boards to ensure strong governance, because an organization's success ultimately comes down to strong leadership. That may include sourcing candidates to consider for the board of directors or advisory board members.

                "Who is the leader? Do you believe in the leader? Are they someone inspiring the team to move forward?" Coape-Arnold said.

                What nonprofits need

                Jane Veron, cofounder and CEO of Acceleration Project, a nonprofit that helps small business owners said that support included identifying 35 processes the organization could eliminate or modify, from onboarding and technology to client data capture.

                For example, instead of having her team read through notes on a client's business challenges, Apollo is helping build an AI tool to do that work. It's also building asynchronous training tools to streamline consultant onboarding.

                "Apollo helped us identify priorities," Veron said, adding that the list includes "very micro and tactical" fixes.

                Reuben Ogbonna II, the cofounder and executive director of The Marcy Lab School, a one-year program that is an alternative to four-year college, said that meant revamping his school's curriculum to reflect the shifting roles of software engineers.

                He said Apollo's deal team helped them recognize that technologists need to work more closely with business leaders and integrated more business and industry context into the curriculum. The program also included additional cloud fundamentals and foundational DevOps knowledge, based on the team's input, he said.

                That sort of hands-on support is the goal, said Kleinman. "Not just to write some checks and get some photo ops, but to really make this a two-way street with our employees."

                Why pay $330 to run a marathon? Let me try to explain.

                📅 Nov 01, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →
                The author during the 2021 NYC Marathon.

                Veranika Li

                • This summer, I spent $333.11 to register for the 2026 New York City Marathon.
                • Between race registration fees and travel, I spend thousands of dollars a year on endurance events.
                • It's money spent in alignment with my values, which experts say is the way to spend.

                You know the type of person who does run club? The one who wakes up before the sun on a Sunday to stack miles and finishes the run at a coffee shop, still sweating as they're waiting in line captioning their Strava post? That's me. I'm that person.

                I'm also among the group of people who spend a lot of money to safety-pin a number to their shirt and run from a start line to a finish line in exchange for a generic tech tee, a medal, and a banana.

                This summer, I spent $333.11 to register for the 2026 New York City Marathon. I didn't bat an eye at checkout — not because I'm rich and the purchase wasn't significant. I'm not, and it was. But, to borrow one of Ramit Sethi's spending concepts, registration fees for endurance events would be one of my top "Money Dials," which are essentially spending categories that you can either turn up or down. It's how I like to spend my discretionary income, and since I cut back in other areas, I can do so guilt-free, no matter how egregious the registration fee.

                I came up with the idea to write this particular story on a run. It was a Tuesday in June. I know the date because I left myself an eight-second voice memo recording the idea: "Why pay $300 for a marathon — to run 26.2 miles? Let me try to explain," I say, slightly out of breath.

                Why do I pay a lot of money to run marathons? And why the marathon — the 26.2-mile event? Why do I invest not only so much money but also so much time in training and racing? I'm not a professional, and never will be. My time is precious, but my chip time doesn't matter to anyone but me.

                For the past four months, I've pondered those questions — casually at first, and more urgently as the race (and the deadline for this article) approached.

                My first thought was to distinguish between running and racing.

                I picked up long-distance running in my early 20s, after more than a decade of junior tennis and four years of collegiate tennis had left me burned out on the sport. I was living in New York City, where finicky weather, high court fees, and complicated logistics make it difficult to hit a tennis ball, even if I wanted to. Looking for an affordable and efficient way to stay in shape, I turned to running. It was perfect for me: a minimalist who doesn't like stuff or clutter. I already had everything I needed: a pair of Nikes and easy access to a smooth running path.

                As an introvert, running suited me, giving me the time and space to think, plan, ideate, or simply check out of life's stressors. And the more I ran, the better I got at it. My marathon times started to suggest that I was decent at the distance — qualifying for the Boston Marathon is considered the pinnacle for amateur marathoners, a feat I've accomplished a few times — so maybe that's part of the reason I kept running, even if getting better made the activity a little more expensive. We all tend to gravitate toward the things we're good at, don't we?

                If running is meditative, rhythmic, and solitary, racing is exhilarating, hectic, and communal. It's a shared experience. You toe the line with thousands — sometimes tens of thousands — of other runners. But unless you're vying for the podium, you're not competing against them. You're racing the clock and your past self — alongside, not against, thousands of others.

                Preparing for a marathon is challenging. It requires time, patience, and work — stacking miles and workouts for months. It's also incredibly satisfying. By the time race day rolls around, the hard part is done.

                When the gun goes off, the fun begins.

                NYRR

                If running is simple, efficient, and cheap, racing is coordinated, time-consuming, and expensive.

                That $333 entry fee was just the beginning of my expenses for this experience. I bought round-trip flights from Los Angeles and a really expensive pair of "super shoes" for race day. When I'm racing in a city where I don't have friends or family, hotels add up quickly.

                But back to Sethi and his "Money Dials," how you choose to spend your money matters. In fact, studies show that how you spend is oftentimes more important than how much you spend.

                Sethi's point is that, no matter your Money Dial — fitness, travel, experiences, or relationships — you can build a life that allows you to "spend extravagantly and unapologetically on the things that truly matter," while cutting costs "mercilessly" on the things that don't matter to you.

                Simply put: Spend on things that make you happy; don't spend on things that aren't important to you.

                The 2026 New York City Marathon will be my 21st marathon. I keep track in the Notes app on my phone, recording my times, what I ate the night before, how many gels I consumed, and other random tidbits from the training block or race day.

                What you get out of the race is entirely up to you. Your goal can be to run the fastest you ever have — a personal record, or "PR" — or it can be to simply cross the line with a smile on your face.

                Of all the races I've done, the New York City Marathon is my favorite by far. Nearly 60,000 runners gather in Staten Island on the first Sunday of November to run through the city's five boroughs, absorbing high fives and hearty cheers from the millions of New Yorkers lining streets.

                Anything can happen over the course of 26.2 miles, another component of the marathon's charm. You could cramp up and blow up. You could get an assist from a tailwind and negative split.

                It's nearly impossible to have a perfect day, but sometimes race day magic strikes.

                See you out there. Let's dial it up.

That delay opened the door for other brands to step in with stronger devices. We’ve rounded up the best color e-readers, and here are the ones that stood out.

                Color e-reader price increases

                This year has not been good for tech prices. Due to the global memory crisis, prices are increasing on tablets, phones, laptops, and even e-readers. Three out of the four color e-readers on this list increased in price this year. The only e-reader to avoid a price hike was the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft.

                Temper your color expectations

                An e-reader's color won't be quite as vibrant as a tablet's or physical book's. Credit: Samantha Mangino / Mangino

                Having tested my way through a lot of e-readers — and now color e-readers — I’ve found a universal truth: While the colors are accurate, they often look a bit washed out.                 The Beats 360 are eye-catching and impressively customizable, but does the listening experience match up?

                📅 Nov 01, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

                If you don't like the look of the Beats 360 headphones, you might as well click out of this review now.

                That's not to say these headphones are only as good as their appearance — they do have their strengths — but if the many colorways Beats started teasing back in June via World Cup players wasn't enough of a hint, a big part of the allure of these Beats are how they look.

                After spending a couple of weeks with these headphones, and switching out many an ear cushion and head band, I found myself more impressed with some aspects of these headphones, and surprisingly let down in others. While a solid first attempt at this concept, I have some notes — so let's get into it.

                Beats 360 at a glance

                The pink/blue combo demanded a cute background. Credit: Bethany Allard / Mashable

                The new flagship headphones from Beats run for $349.99 (the same intro price as the Beats Studio Pro) and come with the following features:

                • Battery life: 32 hours per charge

                • Active noise cancellation: Yes

                • Microphones: Nine, with eight dedicated to ANC

                • IP rating: IPX4

                • Connection: Bluetooth 5.3, one-touch pairing for Apple and Google Fast Pair for Android users

                • Colors: Black, cloud, sky, pink

                The design of the Beats 360 can't be beat (so far)

                The replaceable components meant allowed me to rock an all pink look. Credit: Bethany Allard / Mashable

                The Beats 360 aren't the first over-ear headphones to do swappable components: Dyson's OnTrac headphones launched with replaceable ear plates and cushions back in 2024. They did, however, also cost $499.99 and are less suited to using during exercise than the Beats.

                The Beats cushion sets are the main draw of their design. The headphones themselves come in four different colors: black, cloud (cream), pink, and sky (light blue). Each headphone will come with its corresponding color in the Performance Knit cushion set, which closely resembles that found on the AirPods Max 2.

                SEE ALSO: The 5 most comfortable headphones we've ever tested

                You'll also have the option of purchasing an additional Performance Knit set in one of six different colors: black, cloud, pink, sky, navy, and volt (a neon green-yellow). Then there are two shades of the UltraPlush cushion set, which comes in black and cloud. The UltraPlush is the same faux leather material used on the Beats Studio Pro (and found on most over-ear headphones). That is to say, they're plenty comfortable for longer periods of wear and a nice alternative if you want to reserve the Performance Knit cushions for more high-activity use. All additional kits are priced at $49.99, but launch pricing has these marked down 80% for just $9.99.

                The de-cushioned Beats surrounded by three cushioning options. Credit: Bethany Allard / Mashable

                It's plenty simple to swap out the cushions, which is why I was surprised by the case. These headphones encourage you to swap them out for different uses throughout the day, yet the magnetic closure case didn't consistently shut properly with an additional cushion set — sometimes it closed just fine, and sometimes I found myself needing to place the headphones and the components in the case just so if I didn't want it to hang open.

                With the right positioning of the extra cushions, the case closed without issue. Credit: Bethany Allard / Mashable But sometimes, despite my best efforts, the case refused to close. Credit: Bethany Allard / Mashable

                Another oversight in the design I didn't love was the lack of a headphone jack and lack of USB-C listening functionality. It's not the end of the world, but it can limit listening options, especially while traveling or for anyone interested in lossless audio — a feature supported by the Beats Studio Pro.

                Where the Beats 360 could definitely do better

                The out-of-box sound on a pair of headphones could literally sound like thousands of angels singing in my ears, but if I'm paying $349.99, I would like the option to adjust my own sound signature. Maybe I want one less angel singing!

                It's a concept Apple seems to understand with the recent iOS 27 update, which finally gave the AirPods Pro 3 a custom equalizer, but these Beats were left out of the software update.

                Adjustable audio would've gone a long way for these customizable headphones. Credit: Bethany Allard / Mashable

                It's unfortunate, especially because the sound on these headphones not only didn't have the whole angel thing going on — it sounded kind of flat and bland, which feels decidedly un-Beats-like. The brand is known for its pumping bass, but here, the mids and vocals take center stage. Case in point: I was not bopping my head along to Lorde's "Supercut," which is a feat I frankly didn't know was possible. On a different point in the genre spectrum, Joni Mitchell's "Both Sides Now" sounded predictably beautiful because it's a Joni Mitchell song — the balance of sound, however, leaned too heavily on her vocals and shrank the guitar into the background. I found myself itching to adjust the equalizer settings while listening to the track.

                The ANC isn't bad

                Faring better than the sound is the ANC. Though it won't create the cocoon of silence some of Mashable's favorite noise-cancelling headphones are capable of, they'll definitely dim the sounds of a student-packed cafe playing loud punk music (trust me). That said, mid-range priced headphones are facing some serious competition from budget headphones these days, which are getting better and better at providing ANC that punches above its weight class.

                The combo of the UltraPlush cushions and ANC made these headphones great for work. Credit: Bethany Allard / Mashable

                There's also the presence of some hissing that's somewhat noticeable without music playing — it's not nearly as loud as some cheaper pairs of headphones, but if you're sensitive to ANC that hisses, it's worth noting.

                Are the Beats 360 worth it?

                At this point, the Beats 360 don't quite have the 360 appeal that they could with a few small changes. The component customization makes it easy to envision a world where these are the headphones people take to the gym instead of AirPods Max, while still being a great pair of headphones to use for work, school, commuting — true all-arounders.

                But middling ANC, OK sound, and zero equalizer for $350 makes it hard to recommend these wholeheartedly to the majority of folks, especially when cheaper headphones can manage all of the above, even if they don't feature the same customization. I anticipate that gym rats will love them — I look forward to the next iteration when the rest of us can, too.

                Voice cloning scams: How to protect yourself from audio deepfakes

                📅 Nov 01, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

                Your phone rings, and without thinking, you answer it. It's your spouse. Or your grandma. Maybe the friend you're always posting TikToks with online. And they're asking for your help. 

                They've been in a car accident, and you have to provide some personal information as their emergency contact. They're in jail and need you to bail them out. Or maybe it's even simpler than that: Grandma can't log into her account and needs to send you a code. Can you please read it to her? 

                The familiar lilt of their voices catch you off guard — only none of them are real. 

                Their voices have been cloned, and malicious actors are donning their audio likenesses to scam you out of your personal information, and sometimes cold, hard cash. That number is growing, making even more people susceptible to the deceptive tech, but there are very simple ways to protect yourself and your loved ones.  

                Scroll through TikTok, and you'll come across hundreds of stories detailing tales concocted by scammers to impersonate your loved ones. In one such video with more than 450,000 views, a young woman writes that her mother was nearly scammed by an imposter who imitated her grandmother's voice. The only way they caught it? Grandma is no longer alive. 

                Scams are on the rise. In 2025, Americans lost around $148.2 billion to digital crimes, a jump of more than 25 percent from the year before. Recent data from digital security company NordVPN found that a growing number of scammers are pitching voice scam services to bad actors on dark web forums and Telegram channels. Sales pitches for voice cloning services rose sevenfold in the last two years, reported NordVPN.

                Why more people are getting fooled by audio scams 

                One reason that number keeps ticking up is the proliferation of sophisticated — but more importantly accessible — generative AI tools, explained Marijus Briedis, CTO at NordVPN. 

                "Some years ago, a cloned voice had something slightly off about it, and most people could hear it. That is gone now," Briedis said. 

                Advanced technology is only one part of the growing scam industry, however. Briedis explained that such tools are being increasingly packaged, priced, and sold directly to the Average Joe. 

                Voice cloning tools, previously a standalone novelty tech, are now sold as a single feature in all-encompassing, common criminal toolkits, or "scam kits," experts told Mashable. These kits include access to legitimate generative AI tools via jailbroken accounts, troves of personal data, and other features sold at increasingly affordable prices. 

                Credit: Cole Kan / Mashable / Getty

                For example, a recent study of dark web marketplaces conducted by NordVPN found that a hacked ElevenLabs Scale account — complete with unlimited voice cloning — sold for just $150. An ElevenLabs API key was going for a mere $8.

                Scam networks no longer need technologically savvy hackers or technologists. Just about anyone with a computer can do it. And that means you have to be prepared. 

                Step 1: Know the threat and make a plan 

                "When anyone can run the attack, volume becomes the strategy," Briedis said. "No single attempt has to be perfect. There just have to be a lot of them."

                But asking someone to be on alert all the time is unfair, Briedis said. Up until now, the mantra has been: "Every message, every video, every call. Get it wrong once and that is the one that counts," Briedis explained. "Nobody holds that standard across a lifetime, and most security advice assumes they will."

                As an alternative, users can prepare themselves, and their community, to be able to step up when the moment calls. 

                Credit: Cole Kan/Mashable/Getty

                Prepare your contacts

                Eyal Elazar, head of market Intelligence for online merchant security business Riskified, described effective scam preparation as being a "digital ambassador" for your inner circle. 

                It begins with a little research. Find and save verified contact information for important callers, such as your bank, insurance company, or family lawyers. You can use this to cross reference callers later.

                Then, talk to your circles about what a legitimate phone call would look like. Know who lists you as an emergency contact, and in what contexts. Are you a beneficiary on an account, and, if so, what do you need to know?

                Set a code word

                Most experts Mashable spoke to recommend creating a code word that you can use with friends and family to confirm who they are. Don't share this anywhere online. "Sounds silly right up until the day it does not," Briedis said.

                Filter out the red flags  

                There are also common scam requests that are instant red flags, experts told Mashable. Any demand for money over the phone is suspicious. There are more specific tells, too: 

                • Requests to read a code, sent via text or email, over the phone

                • Requests for passwords or other log-in credentials 

                • Demands for payment via gift cards, wire transfers, crypto exchanges, and payment apps

                • Suggestions to initiate a wire transfer over a voice note, a phone call, or a voicemail

                • Demands of ransom

                • Law enforcement dealings conducted via phone call

                Step 2: Putting down the phone can stop a scammer.

                "AI isn’t inventing new scams, but it's removing the tells we’ve learned to look for in the old ones," said Donnie Hasseltine, chief information security officer at Arkstone Defense. 

                It can be hard to discern the small audio tells that make your loved ones' voice truly theirs, especially when an individual is up against social engineering that forces urgency and stirs panic. 

                So, the next piece of advice is to hang up on your friends or "friends." 

                Yes, this may cause some drama in the group chat. But if you can't always tell when a voice is real or cloned, it's best to cut them off and reset. 

                If someone you personally know was supposedly on the other line, call them back on the number you're used to before agreeing to anything. If it's a bank or your workplace, call a listed number on an official website, the back of a credit card, or a piece of mail. Many institutions are already keenly aware of common phone scams that target customers. 

                "Stop judging the content and change the channel instead," Breidis urged. 

                SEE ALSO: Have you been impacted by a scam or security breach?

                Step 3: Slow down.

                The last, and most simple, piece of advice is to take a breath. Experts told Mashable that urgency is the number one red flag that may indicate you are the target of a scam, e.g., someone claiming to be from the electricity company demanding money immediately in exchange for keeping your power on. That supposed urgency also sets you up to be more susceptible to scammers. 

                Andrew Jones, co-founder of Adaptive Security, said that a manufactured sense of urgency as well as a demand for secrecy are the two factors found in nearly every successful scam he has studied. 

                "Nothing is so urgent that it can’t wait for you to verify it," Hasseltine agreed. 

                So don't give in to the rush. Slow down, hang up the phone, and ask someone else to weigh in. 

                And it bears repeating: Never. Send. Cash. 

                Want more tech and digital culture news delivered to your inbox daily or sent straight to your device? Sign up for Mashable's Top Stories newsletter or get Mashable push alerts today.

                Already been scammed? Here's what to do.

                If a scammer has already gotten hold of your personal information or money, act fast:

                1. Block the scammer so they can't reach out again.

                2. Cut off their access to your bank account or payment method, if you provided that information. Call your bank immediately. If you sent a wire transfer or gift card, contact the issuer and tell the company you have been scammed. Change your passwords. Freeze your credit.

                3. Report your stolen information. Go to IdentityTheft.gov to create a government-recommended recovery plan. Report the scam to the Social Security Administration’s fraud hotline if you handed over your SSN.

                4. Stay calm. The vast majority of Americans have been scammed in one way or another. There is help out there, and you can prepare your defenses for next time.

                Landline phones will switch off across Britland in 100 days, no extensions – Openreach

                📅 Nov 01, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

                Openreach has issued a stark reminder to customers that the legacy phone network is being officially switched off on January 31, and says the deadline will not be postponed.

                The infrastructure arm of BT Group, Britain’s biggest telecoms biz, circulated the warning this week in a letter to comms providers that use its network to deliver their services.

                It informs them that any customers still on legacy public switched telephone network (PSTN) connections are at risk of disruption when these are retired at the end of January, 2027.

                The switch-off could affect businesses and consumers alike. Beyond the plain old telephone, systems that rely on PSTN connectivity include point-of-sale terminals, fire and security alarms, and personal care alarms for elderly and vulnerable people.

                The move is part of a wider government scheme to get the UK onto all-digital high-speed networks running on fiber-optic infrastructure, and the legacy phone service - with its dependency on copper cabling - was standing in the way.

                Many households have now ditched landline handsets and instead use only mobile phones, yet for those who still want a landline, the changeover means plugging the phone into the back of a broadband router to access a Digital Voice service.

                Openreach has been planning this move for the best part of a decade. It has already pushed back the deadline at least once, after the government asked telecoms providers not to force vulnerable customers who use phone-network systems such as TeleCare to switch until fixes are in place.

                Nevertheless, public awareness seems low that analog phone services will soon be disconnected. "Openreach and all providers need to coordinate a much more cohesive campaign that reaches customers directly," said telecoms analyst Paolo Pescatore at PP Foresight.

                "TV, billboards and newspaper advertising should reinforce a consistent message, supported by targeted letters, calls and door-to-door support for older and vulnerable people who need extra help," he told The Register.

                "Customers need to understand what is changing, what action to take, and who will help them. Providers must take responsibility for ensuring people remain safely connected, especially those who rely on their landline or a care alarm."

                Caroline Abrahams, charity director at Age UK, agreed.

                "With only three months to go, the digital landline switchover is entering a critical final phase. Most people have moved over without major problems, but nobody who relies on their landline or TeleCare should be left behind," she told us.

                "Anyone with concerns should contact their provider, but the responsibility cannot rest with customers alone. Providers must not give up on people who have not responded. They need to keep trying to reach them and offer practical, individual support, recognizing that some may be unwell, living with dementia, worried about scams or without anyone nearby to help."

                Openreach has a webpage with information regarding the switch-off. This advises consumers to call their service provider as soon as possible to ensure service is not interrupted.

                The company previously told The Register that customers without a fiber connection will likely be switched to SOTAP for Analog (Single Order Transitional Access Product), where equipment is installed in the local telephone exchange to allow them to continue to use their old phone line as before.

                Openreach has warned that commercial customers delaying migration risk significant disruption and unnecessary costs - leaving it until the last minute could make it harder to secure the requisite engineering support before the deadline hits.

                "Businesses and organizations that delay action are making things harder for themselves," said James Lilley, Openreach Director of All-IP.

                "The straightforward migrations have largely been completed. What's left are the complex connections that underpin critical operations, requiring careful planning, supplier coordination, and thorough testing. We are urging businesses to act now, audit their remaining analog services, and work with their communications provider on a migration plan today."

                Earlier this year, the firm tried to drive home the message by announcing it was stepping up its charges to service providers and companies still operating legacy business lines, who will by now be paying double the rental cost compared to last year. ®

                AI Is Changing the Junior Developer Career Path. Here's How CS Students Can Adapt

                📅 Nov 01, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

                Ten years ago, the standard advice to a computer science student was simple: learn a language, build projects, collect a few frameworks, and apply for junior roles. Junior roles were where people got paid to learn the craft.

                AI coding agents are putting that ladder under pressure. Today's tools don't just autocomplete a line. They read a whole repository, edit several files, run commands, and retry when tests fail. The routine work that used to fill a junior developer's first year is exactly the work these tools handle best.

                I'm a computer science student, and I feel this shift every time I open an AI coding tool. It can scaffold a feature in minutes that would have taken me an afternoon. But I've also caught myself accepting code I couldn't explain, and then getting stuck when it broke. That gap between "it runs" and "I understand why it runs" is what pushed me to dig into the research, and to change how I study.

                This article looks at what the evidence says and what a student can do about it.

                What the Data Says About Early-Career Developers

                Researchers at the Stanford Digital Economy Lab analyzed payroll records from ADP, the largest US payroll provider. They found that workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations saw a 16 percent relative decline in employment, even after controlling for firm-level shocks. Employment for more experienced workers in the same occupations stayed stable or kept growing. Software developers were one of the example occupations the paper highlights.

                Two details matter for students. First, the researchers found that adjustment happens mainly through employment rather than pay, so the problem is fewer openings, not lower salaries. Second, the declines were concentrated in occupations where AI is more likely to automate work than to augment it. A summary from ADP Research walks through the same findings in plain language.

                Read that carefully: it doesn't say programming is over. It says that tasks that are easy to specify and easy to automate are the ones disappearing from entry-level hiring. Your goal is to be useful at everything around those tasks.

                The Trap: Shipping Before Understanding

                Here is the uncomfortable part. The tools that make you fast can also stop you from learning.

                In a randomized controlled trial with 52 software engineers learning an unfamiliar Python async library, the AI-assisted group scored about 50% on a follow-up quiz, versus about 67% for the group that coded by hand. The biggest gap was on debugging questions. The AI group finished only about two minutes sooner, a difference that was not statistically significant.

                The outcome also depended on how people used the assistant, not just whether they used it. People who asked for explanations and worked through the reasoning retained more than people who handed over the whole task.

                The sample is small and the task was narrow, so treat it as a warning sign rather than a law. But it matches what many learners feel: you can complete an assignment without being able to redo it tomorrow.

                The Second Trap: Code That Works but Isn't Safe

                A working feature and a safe feature are different things. Veracode tested more than 100 language models on 80 coding tasks. The models produced functional code but introduced security vulnerabilities in 45 percent of cases. Java was the worst, with failure rates above 70 percent, and models failed to defend against cross-site scripting in 86 percent of relevant cases. Help Net Security's coverage summarizes the details.

                The finding worth remembering: Veracode found that larger models did not perform meaningfully better than smaller ones, which points to a systemic issue rather than something scale will fix. The AI will happily write a login system. It won't reliably tell you what's wrong with it. That judgment has to come from you.

                Where You Can Still Stand Out

                If generating routine code gets cheap, these skills gain value:

                • Reading code critically. Reviewing a diff you didn't write is now a daily job. Practice by reading open-source pull requests.
                • Debugging from first principles. Form a hypothesis, find evidence, narrow the cause. This is exactly the skill the trial above found weakest in heavy AI users.
                • Security basics. Know the OWASP Top 10 well enough to spot injection, broken access control, and bad session handling by eye.
                • Turning vague problems into clear specs. "Users leave at checkout" isn't a ticket. Someone has to make it one.
                • Testing. Write tests that try to break the AI's code, not tests that confirm it.
                • Explaining your decisions. In interviews and code reviews, "why does this work?" is the question that separates understanding from copying.

                A Learning Routine That Keeps You Honest

                Try a simple loop I call Sketch, Delegate, Break, Rebuild:

                1. Sketch. Before opening any AI tool, write your own plan on paper: routes, data model, who can access what, what could go wrong.
                2. Delegate. Ask the AI for an implementation, and ask it to explain its choices and list edge cases.
                3. Break. Try to make it fail. Send bad input, log in as the wrong user, delete a required field.
                4. Rebuild. Close the chat and re-implement one important piece from memory.

                Steps 3 and 4 feel slower, and that's the point. They are where the learning the trial measured actually happens.

                What to Build Now

                Portfolio projects that show only "I generated an app" are getting less convincing. Stronger signals include:

                • a project with a written design note explaining your decisions
                • a test suite you wrote to challenge generated code
                • a short security review of your own app
                • a commit history that shows you debugging real problems

                Employers and clients can't easily fake-check understanding, so show it openly.

                The Bottom Line

                AI won't remove the need for people who understand software, but it is raising the bar for what an entry-level person must bring. Use the tools heavily for speed, exploration, and drafts. Just make sure the understanding stays in your head, not only in the chat history. The students who do both will be the ones who look like low-risk hires when the ladder gets narrower.

                Turn Customer Questions Into a Marketing Research System

                📅 Nov 01, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

                Hero image: Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

                A sales team answers the same implementation question in several calls. Support explains a related limitation in tickets. Marketing publishes another broad trend article because the repeated question never becomes a research brief.

                The organization already has useful signals. What it lacks is a process for turning them into public knowledge without exposing private information, mistaking a loud customer for the whole market, or allowing an AI summary to erase the original concern.

                Disclosure: I am the founder and CEO of INSIDEA, an Elite HubSpot Partner. This article reflects practical experience and independent research. It is not sponsored by HubSpot or any other company mentioned.

                I would build a question-to-research workflow with separate collection, protection, clustering, and validation stages. The model below is a proposed editorial system. It does not require copying all customer communications into a model, and no private customer material was accessed to develop the examples.

                Collect questions for a defined purpose

                Begin with an approved research purpose: identify recurring uncertainties that useful public content could address. That is narrower than collecting everything customers say or using private conversations as an unrestricted source of marketing material.

                Select appropriate inputs through the organization's access and information-handling process. A reviewed question submitted by a salesperson can be enough to start. A full call recording or ticket export may contain far more information than the editorial task needs.

                Define what should not enter the research queue: credentials, personal details, account-specific secrets, confidential commercial terms, and material whose permitted use is unclear. When the useful question can be separated from private context, retain the general question rather than the entire interaction. When it cannot, hold it for appropriate review.

                Preserve the question before summarizing it

                A summary can make a specific concern look generic. A buyer asking how reporting history survives a CRM migration is not simply asking for a migration guide. A support question about an unexpected billing association is not merely interest in automation.

                Retain an approved, appropriately protected version of the question and a separate editorial interpretation. Record the context needed to understand it: the decision being made, the audience role, the relevant constraints, and the source type. Avoid retaining identifiable detail that does not serve the purpose.

                The W3C provenance overview offers a general foundation for tracing origins and transformations. A question record inspired by that idea should explain where the editorial interpretation came from, without exposing restricted source material to everyone who reads the content backlog.

                Separate frequency from importance

                Repeated questions can reveal a content gap, but repetition is not the same as market prevalence. A large customer, a busy account team, or one support incident can dominate the available record. A rare question can also concern a high-consequence decision.

                Track counts with their denominator and collection window where feasible. Distinguish repeated messages from distinct people, accounts, and underlying problems. A thread with ten replies should not automatically become ten independent expressions of demand.

                Add consequence and decision relevance as separate review dimensions. A question that affects security, migration integrity, or contractual understanding may deserve careful explanation even when it appears infrequently. The research agenda should combine audience need and consequence rather than rank topics solely by mention count.

                Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

                Cluster by uncertainty, not merely vocabulary

                Two questions can use similar words while requiring different answers. How do we automate a handoff and how do we prove a handoff completed are not the same problem. Conversely, different terminology can describe the same underlying uncertainty.

                Ask the clustering process to identify the decision, missing knowledge, relevant constraints, and expected answer type. Use AI to propose groupings, then have a domain reviewer inspect them. Keep the original approved questions available for that review so a tidy label does not hide a false merge.

                Allow a question to belong to more than one research category when that reflects the problem. A migration concern may involve identity, reporting, and change management. Forced single-label classification can create artificial boundaries that make the resulting content less useful to the person who asked.

                Turn clusters into research briefs

                A useful brief states the audience, the decision, what existing material fails to explain, the evidence needed, the proposed contribution, and the limitations. It should also state what the article will not attempt to answer.

                For a hypothetical reporting-history question, the brief might compare migration approaches, explain what needs testing, and provide an acceptance checklist. It should not promise to resolve every account's data architecture or imply that a generic import procedure preserves every historical relationship.

                Google's people-first content guidance gives a usefulness-oriented editorial reference. A question-derived brief still needs original analysis and suitable evidence. The existence of a customer question does not establish the correctness of the answer the team wants to publish.

                Research independently of the source conversation

                A customer or salesperson may describe a product capability inaccurately. An internal anecdote may omit conditions that change the conclusion. Treat the question as a reason to investigate, not as proof of the proposed answer.

                Verify product claims through current primary documentation and clearly label account-specific behavior. If the public evidence is insufficient, narrow the article or state the uncertainty. Do not imply firsthand testing when the work is documentary analysis.

                The NIST AI Risk Management Framework provides a general risk-management perspective. Applying review to generated summaries and research claims is a local proposal, not a certification. The team should record what it verified and where a qualified specialist or account-specific test remains necessary.

                Protect people when converting examples

                Removing a name is not always sufficient to make a story anonymous. A distinctive industry, timeline, system combination, or numerical result may identify a customer to people familiar with the situation. Review the whole example, not only the obvious identifiers.

                Where permission is absent, write a synthetic scenario that illustrates the mechanism and label it explicitly. Do not combine real customer details into an invented case study and present it as practical experience. A useful hypothetical example does not need an implied client pedigree.

                Keep original evidence restricted to its appropriate audience. Public drafts should contain only approved material. If a writer needs to verify a sensitive detail, route the question to the owner rather than expanding access to the entire source conversation for convenience.

                Keep AI access narrower than editorial ambition

                HubSpot's AI-settings guide describes feature access and data-source controls. A setting that permits AI use does not settle whether a particular conversation should be used for public research.

                Start with an approved, minimized input set. Test the workflow using synthetic questions before adding real material. Check whether summaries retain unnecessary identifiers, whether clusters reveal restricted details, and whether generated briefs invent frequency or customer outcomes.

                Do not change CRM access, model-training settings, or data-sharing permissions merely to make topic generation easier. Those are separate governance decisions. If the research workflow needs broader access, identify the missing requirement and obtain the appropriate review rather than treating it as a normal editorial shortcut.

                Prioritize by usefulness and ability to answer

                A topic can be commercially attractive and still be a poor choice if the team lacks evidence to answer it well. Use a review matrix that separates audience relevance, decision consequence, available evidence, originality, and maintenance burden.

                Keep those judgments explainable. An arbitrary weighted score can make subjective assumptions look objective. A short written rationale often tells the editorial team more than a decimal ranking nobody can defend.

                Prioritize questions where the organization can add a distinct contribution: a clear explanation of a confusing boundary, a practical test, a comparison of tradeoffs, or a reusable worksheet. Avoid turning every cluster into another broad introduction. Several questions may be answered better by improving one existing resource than by publishing several overlapping articles.

                Return the answer to the teams that supplied the question

                Public publishing is only one destination. Sales and support teams should be able to find the approved explanation, understand its limits, and use it where appropriate. A content program loses value when useful answers remain buried in a marketing calendar.

                Provide a short internal summary of the resource's purpose, suitable audience, date checked, and situations requiring specialist review. Do not instruct teams to send the link automatically to every contact who uses a matching word. Context and relationship still matter.

                Collect feedback on whether the answer resolves the actual concern. A salesperson may find that buyers still need a decision table. Support may identify an omitted edge case. Treat that as evidence for revision, while verifying any new factual claim before it enters the public resource.

                Measure resolved uncertainty, not just topic volume

                Useful measures include briefs accepted for research, questions answered by existing content, recurring misunderstandings after publication, verified reuse by internal teams, and qualified conversations where the resource helped clarify scope. Define the evidence for each measure.

                Do not claim that every reduction in support questions was caused by the article. Product changes, staffing, customer mix, and seasonality may also matter. Where the relationship cannot be established, report the observation and its limitations.

                The deeper objective is a learning system: customer uncertainty informs research, research produces an inspectable answer, and subsequent questions test whether the explanation was sufficient. AI can help organize the material. Human judgment must still decide what deserves publication and what the evidence can support.

                Build a small loop before automating collection

                Begin with one approved source team, a narrow problem area, and a small set of protected questions. Create a few research briefs, verify the answers, and test whether the resulting resources are useful. Only then consider expanding collection or automation.

                This avoids creating a large sensitive archive before proving the editorial workflow. It also lets the team refine the distinction between a question worth answering publicly and one that belongs in a private customer conversation.

                The future of AI marketing is not limited to generating more content from public trends. A business can use AI to organize what its audience is struggling to understand, then invest in answers that deserve attention. The value comes from the quality of that learning loop, not the size of the question database.

                For a related evidence boundary, see A Five-Part Governance Framework for HubSpot Agent Knowledge Vaults. The framework above addresses a distinct marketing decision rather than repeating that model.

                Sources checked October 21, 2026. All examples are hypothetical. No customer conversations, recordings, tickets, or private CRM data were accessed.

                Recently, he arrived at the Barranquilla police command around the early hours of the morning as 587 police officers and soldiers raided 50 locations across the Caribbean port city and its suburbs in Operation Blindaje 360. A few days earlier, domestic Colombian news outlets had widely publicized a recording intercepted by Colombian police of "Keko", the alleged leader of a gang called "Los del Freseo" boasting that de la Espirella had nothing on him.

                "The Tiger's got nothing. Let him come out, and we'll put lead in him," Keko allegedly said on the recording.

                Then, before dawn, Colombia's president had tracked him down and was face to face with him, all caught on tape.

                According to a video released by his presidential office, El Tigre told Keko the gang leader was "a tough guy on the phone… but the look of the fear on his face matched that of his many victims". The sweep ended with 72 arrests.

                ANTI-CARTEL HARDLINER CHANNELS TRUMP IN BID TO END COLOMBIA'S LEFTIST ERA IN PIVOTAL ELECTION

                The theatrics played to a large audience who long argued that former leftist Gustavo Petros’s policy of pursuing engagement with drug traffickers and through conversation and peace talks had left Colombia more vulnerable to organized crime and further articulation between Colombian and Venezuelan cartels that had been dominating the space left by the power vacuum which emerged from effective law-enforcement control.

                His government is also seeking to reverse former President Gustavo Petro’s "total peace" policy, which pursued negotiations with several armed organizations. Before taking office, de la Espriella announced that he would dismantle key elements of the policy and reactivate arrest warrants against members of illegal armed groups.

                Nearly three months into his term, the 48-year-old lawyer has scrapped his leftist predecessor's "total peace" talks, ordered every armed group treated as a terrorist organization and claims more than 32,000 arrests. He is doing it arm in arm with Washington.

                A dual U.S.-Colombian citizen who lived in Miami before running for president, he has brought Colombia into President Donald Trump's anti-cartel coalition. Last month, he personally handed a guerrilla boss accused of supplying Mexico's Sinaloa Cartel to DEA agents with his hands and feet shackled.

                The prisoner, Geovany Andrés Rojas, alias "Araña," is alleged to have led the "Comandos de la Frontera" dissidents and now faces narco-terrorism charges in Southern California.

                "The option of dialogue is completely exhausted," de la Espriella told troops after his Aug. 7 inauguration. In an Oct. 12 address, he put the tally at 32,503 arrests, 33 ringleaders taken out of action and 679 drug-production sites destroyed or disabled. He has signed more than 100 extradition orders, including five for former armed-group peace negotiators wanted in the U.S. whose handovers the previous government had frozen.

                ‘DONROE’ DOCTRINE AND CONSERVATIVE VICTORIES SQUEEZE CARTELS IN LATIN AMERICA

                The offensive reaches deep into the countryside, where conflict monitor ACLED counted August as the deadliest month for clashes between security forces and armed groups since it began tracking Colombia in 2018. 

                In late August he warned FARC dissident chief Iván Mordisco: "When you least expect it, a bomb is going to fall on you." Two days later, he walked among the bagged bodies of 23 suspected dissidents at an army base in Guaviare, and troops killed the top commander of a paramilitary-rooted trafficking group in La Guajira.

                Colombia became the 19th member of Trump's Shield of the Americas coalition in August, and War Secretary Pete Hegseth said Bogotá had authorized "joint military operations to destroy terrorists and terror networks domestically." The administration has pledged $1 billion in security aid, pending congressional approval, and Marine Gen. Francis Donovan, head of U.S. Southern Command, has toured Colombian bases.

                However, speaking on-camera to Fox News Digital, Colombian Vice President José Manuel Restrepo said while his country is embracing President Donald Trump’s push for a new security alliance across the Western Hemisphere, he drew a clear line on the role American forces would play inside Colombia, saying Colombian troops — not U.S. forces — will carry out operations against the country’s armed groups.

                PENTAGON SENDS HUNDREDS OF ARMY TROOPS TO LATIN AMERICA FOR TRAINING AS DRUG-TRAFFICKING CAMPAIGN EXPANDS

                According to Benjamin Gedan, a senior fellow and director of the Latin America Program at the Stimson Center in Washington who previously served as a South America Director in the White House, the last few years were an outlier:

                "For decades, the United States and Colombia closely cooperated to fight guerrillas and organized crime. Plan Colombia was celebrated by both Republicans and Democrats. The Colombian military is well-trained and battle-tested. Renewed close cooperation between Bogotá and Washington is a cornerstone of the renewed U.S. focus on security in Latin America," he said.

                "Still, flashy military strikes on criminal targets will not answer the mail. These groups are well-armed, well-funded, and thrive in regions with little state presence. Images of criminals in body bags may give the impression of forward progress after the failed strategy of Colombia’s last leader, much as videos of exploding speedboats have become the calling card of the Shield of the Americas. In both cases, a more sophisticated strategy is needed to deal lasting blows to criminal groups," Gedan argued.

                CRIME, KIDNAPPINGS AND DRONE ATTACKS FLAGGED IN US WARNING FOR BORDER REGION

                Oscar Palma, a professor of Security Studies at the University of Rosario in Bogotá, said it is still a little too early to assess the change in policies and affirm they will be fruitful within the Colombian context. "Beyond the policing acts themselves, there is the subjective feeling of security with debates within Colombian society on whether this open war strategy brings more or less security to the population. Many argue that the gangs are acting now more forcefully to defend their territories and business deals, while others believe that a strong police presence will eventually lead to less organized crime."

                Palma said there is a false dichotomy between having to choose all-out war or dialogue in order to achieve peace with groups such as the FARC and other gang leaders: "It is a fiction that you will come to zero combatants simply pursuing one strategy or the other—all-out war will never zero down those combating in the FARC and organized crime just as peace talks, especially if carried out in a misguided policy such as the one led by [Gustavo] Petros, will achieve real results."

                He said, "A better example is the strategy carried out by President [Juán Manuel] Santos during the dealings with the FARC, which led to a much safer Colombia: there were talks, but those were part of a bigger strategy of also fighting these groups with arms and bringing them to justice," he added.

                "There is a wave of freedom, a wave of democracy, a wave of free market… There is a new momentum for the region and we have to take advantage of that momentum. That's what I said to President Trump," Restrepo told Fox News Digital. "If we want to keep and preserve democracy in the region, the Shield of the Americas is going to be the best opportunity to do it."

                The mall isn't just a place for people to buy clothing, food and receive services, but is a "community hub" of mostly women entrepreneurs, as described by a female shop owner.

                "It is kind of an incubator setting where many businesses start in here, and then many succeed and grow and move somewhere else, to a bigger space," Sabri explained to Fox News Digital.

                "You can see [the] Somalis not only integrating in the community, but also prospering," he said. "Somalis are very smart business individuals."

                But the mall's very name — the Karmel Mall of Somalia — along with the overwhelmingly Somali culture inside, raise questions about whether the group is actually assimilating into American society.

                WORKING-CLASS AMERICANS SAY THEIR TOWN IS THE NEXT DEARBORN — AND THEY'VE HAD ENOUGH

                Steven Camerota is the director for research at the Center for Immigration Studies (CIS). He pointed Fox News Digital to a CIS report published in December of last year that describes Somalis as a "struggling group."

                The report shows that more than half of children who live in the homes of Somali-born immigrants in Minnesota live in poverty, compared to only 8% of children living in homes of native-born Minnesotans. Among Somali-born immigrants who have lived in the United States for more than a decade, half cannot speak English "very well." The report says that 89% of Somali households receive some form of welfare, and 39% don't have high school diplomas, compared to only 8% of the native population.

                Camerota argued that across America, assimilation among various foreign-born groups, including Somalis, has dropped, though today's immigration numbers are about the same they were during America's first great wave of immigration.

                In the late 19th- and early 20th-centuries, immigrations from across the world flooded the United States. During that time, immigrants comprised about 15% of America's population, on par with todays numbers. After World War I, restrictive immigration policies that lasted until the 1960s took effect. In more recent history, immigration has ramped up to the tune of one million legal immigrants per year entering the United States, Camerota said.

                MINNESOTA SENATE HOPEFUL WARNS THREAT LEVEL RISING AMID RASH OF SOMALI GANG CRIME, TERROR PLOT

                "So, there are three big things about modern immigration that you can argue greatly hinder assimilation, and it has much less to do with the immigrants, and a lot more to do with just modern conditions," he told Fox News Digital. "The first is technology. You can fly home and visit home for the holidays if you want. In a way that just wouldn't have been possible in 1900, and in terms of costs."

                Camerota noted that the internet allows people access to constant news from home, and the constant ability to stay connected with family and friends via phone and video calls.

                "So this technology, travel and communications is fundamentally different today than in the past. And that likely means that the connection with the home country doesn't become as attenuated as quickly as it would have," he said.

                The attitudes of those who Camerota characterizes as "elites," in academia, government, media and other institutions has also changed. He said there are now dueling theories about the what exactly America is that could be contributing to a lack of assimilation.

                FORMER MN STATE TROOPER TEARS INTO DEMS AS SOMALI GANG VIOLENCE TERRORIZES MINNESOTA: ‘WHERE IS ILHAN OMAR?’

                "So is America essentially a magnificent historical project of democracy and equality and republican government, or is it essentially — most of that's a sham and it's really a racist, sexist, homophobic [and] classist society?" he said. "The immigrants are arriving in a country in many ways that received both those messages, and so this elite attitude which permeates down is just so different than the world of the last great wave of immigration and almost certainly matters a great deal."

                Essentially, Camerota argued, if immigrants adopt the narrative that America is a fundamentally flawed nation, there is little reason for them to assimilate.

                "The word assimilation itself is seen as a bad word in many circles. The idea that immigrants are supposed to shed their their old culture and become American is now seen as a kind of for some — I don't want to say universally for all — but some fraction of it at least, as an undesirable Anglo conformity," he continued.

                "We are living in a country that can't really agree itself about its own history, let alone agree on what it wants from the immigrants."

                The third important fact to assimilation in Camerota's mind is the sheer number of immigrants coming to the United States.

                ALARMING FRAUD TREND PUTS SMALL-TOWN MOSQUE WITH INDUSTRY AND FOREIGN GOVT TIES IN FOCUS: ‘OUR MOTHERLAND NOW’

                "The last point is numbers," he said. "So, we're at a record high now, right? 15% of the population is foreign born. It's matched the levels of between 1890 and 1910 ... during the last peak of the last great wave. But the one question then has to be asked, what happened then?"

                He said the immigration restriction of the mid 20th-century necessarily resulted in assimilation, as immigrants could not endlessly build enclaves for more and more foreign-born residents, as is happening today.

                "I think it's pretty clear it likely played a very big role in facilitating the assimilation of the immigrants," he said, suggesting that a similar immigration restriction could have the same effect if implemented now.

                If you like playing daily word games like Wordle, then Hurdle is a great game to add to your routine.

                There are five rounds to the game. The first round sees you trying to guess the word, with correct, misplaced, and incorrect letters shown in each guess. If you guess the correct answer, it'll take you to the next hurdle, providing the answer to the last hurdle as your first guess. This can give you several clues or none, depending on the words. For the final hurdle, every correct answer from previous hurdles is shown, with correct and misplaced letters clearly shown.

                An important note is that the number of times a letter is highlighted from previous guesses does necessarily indicate the number of times that letter appears in the final hurdle.

                Xbox Manager: AI Already Being Used In Xbox Game Development - And Throughout the Game Industry

                📅 Nov 01, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →
                Should generative AI be used for videogame development? Brandon Stirrup, a strategy manager at Xbox, claims Xbox is already using AI, reports Engadget. And he also says that those who say they aren't are merely "pretending." Stirrup deactivated his social media account shortly after (though his posts have been archived elsewhere), igniting conversations about what role generative AI actually has or should have in game development. In some ways, it would be unsurprising to learn that Xbox is using AI to the extent that Stirrup implies. Xbox recently announced the formation of Xbox Labs at least in part as a response to a rising trend of AI-coded game ports; the announcement heavily implied that the new team would use AI as well but didn't say it outright. Xbox owner Microsoft is also a major player in AI development... Developers including Capcom, Square Enix, Sega, Nexon and Activision have all either used AI in their games or pledged to do so. Fortnite developer Epic Games has been particularly up-front about its AI use, and CEO Tim Sweeney has aggressively promoted it on social media... On the other hand, there are large pockets of the game industry vocally opposed to generative AI. Notably, these tend to be smaller, independent studios without shareholders to impress by touting the cost-savings of AI. These studios include Tunic publisher Finji, Stardew Valley developer ConcernedApe and Clickolding developer Strange Scaffold, among many more. Due to the sheer number and variety of game studios, it's impossible to say just how much of the industry actually uses AI at this point, but claims that "everyone" is using it are clearly false. There's a similar divide among players about whether generative AI should be embraced or avoided at all costs. While some simply accept AI as part of games going forward, others have pledged to avoid games that use the technology outright due to its environmental costs, labor issues or pure aesthetic preference. That's led to the popularity of tools like a browser extension that makes Steam's AI disclosures more visible and grassroots efforts by developers to implement labels certifying their games as AI-free... Many players and developers alike justify the use of AI in generating code, even if they're opposed to it in other areas. "Gaming is the only industry slow-walking the transition," Xbox's Stirrup allegedly said, "because users have negative sentiment. Everyone else accepts reality." "Gaming is the only industry pretending to not use AI."

                Binance Replenishes 90% of Stolen $6.3B, Pledges They'll Cover It All, Reopen Sunday

                📅 Nov 01, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →
                "We've now replenished 90% of the stolen assets, and we're committed to covering the remaining 10%," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng posted on X, adding that "Our users will not bear the financial impact of this incident." "Binance said it was able to replace the funds taken in the record hack by using company money to buy new tokens," reports NBC News: The remaining 10% consists of tokens that are less liquid, meaning they may take longer to buy, it said in a statement posted on X... Binance said it has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The money spent re-buying tokens came from using part of its $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users, a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund, and the company's own corporate treasury, it said on X. NBC News reports that the FBI blames the breach on a North Korea-sponsored group known as TraderTraitor: Members of [TraderTraitor] were observed by law enforcement converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ethereum, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expects "further laundering" of the assets through the use of related technology... After the hack, the exchange stopped allowing customers to withdraw their funds, but it said Saturday it was still on track to reopen withdrawals Sunday. CNBC reports: The world's largest crypto exchange initially said the hack may involve "a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." However, Co-CEO Richard Teng later said the attack involved a more complex process rather than the misuse of a single engineer's permissions. The New York Times describes what happened when Binance first spotted "a multibillion-dollar deluge of digital coins" pouring out of its accounts: As the news spread, Binance's top executives put together an informal war room on Wea, the company's internal messaging system, with about 100 participants, including specialized cryptocurrency tracers and security personnel. They eventually transitioned to a mass conference call, with 100 boxes on the screen, where employees took turns muting and then unmuting, communicating in a mixture of English and Chinese. Among them was He Yi, Binance's co-chief executive, who is seven months pregnant, and worked through the night from her base in Abu Dhabi, taking a call at 3 a.m. local time.... Much of the drama played out in public. Almost all crypto transactions are recorded on the blockchain, a ledger of money movements that anyone can look up. That meant crypto analysts could see funds leaving Binance in real time... North Koreans have targeted crypto companies for years, using the proceeds of those thefts to fund its nuclear program, according to Western officials. The hackers have developed increasingly complex strategies to steal crypto and launder the proceeds, a painstaking endeavor that can take months to complete. In a blog post on Friday, Chainalysis said the attackers had deployed "laundering patterns we have not seen before," conducting thousands of transactions over a short period, probably with the help of automation. At the same time, Binance's colleagues in the industry mobilized to intercept some of the laundered crypto. Certain digital coin issuers can freeze funds, allowing them to halt a money-laundering operation in its tracks. Soon after the hack, Tether and Circle, two major issuers, announced that they had frozen stashes of their own coins that the hackers had seized from Binance, a combined total of more than $2 billion in crypto. Binance is now working to gain access to those funds, the company said. But $2.4 billion in crypto is already "beyond any issuer's reach," according to [blockchain intelligence firmm] TRM. The article also includes President Trump's reaction when asked Friday about the breach. "I've always felt it was a little bit dangerous. But they say they have it pretty much under control. We'll see."

                French Lawmakers Back Per-Gigabyte Internet Traffic Tax

                📅 Oct 31, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →
                Companies like Google, Netflix, TikTok, and Meta may soon owe the French government, reports Tom's Hardware: France has approved a proposed tax that aims to tax the amount of internet data per gigabyte sent to French users in the country... According to minutes released by the National Assembly, members voted 11-10 in support of the motion on October 30 — which now means the new law has been added to the country's next budget, despite major opposition from the government side and the finance committee rapporteur. The latest amendment, introduced by socialist lawmaker Laurent Lhardit, could see content providers pay €0.055 (roughly $0.06) to the government for every gigabyte of content distributed to French users. With approximately 154 million users and counting in France, the proposal's authors say such a tax could generate around €10 billion ($11.2 billion) in annual revenue for the government. The said proposal, though yet to be passed as it must survive further parliamentary scrutiny, aims at companies that generate substantial internet traffic as opposed to taxing their advertising revenue, profits and subscriptions. Its explanatory notes particularly mention Google, Meta, Netflix, Amazon, and content delivery network Akamai as major potential contributors. Notably, TikTok and other similar platforms could fall under this broader scope depending on how these rules are applied. Internet service providers, including Orange Free and Liad, would be required to measure the volume of data and identify the companies responsible for sending it to French users. The Data will then be collected and submitted quarterly to France's tax administration under the supervision of telecommunications watchdog Arcep. The measure becomes law if it clears the remaining stages of France's budget process, the article points out, "with parliament scheduled to vote on the budget's first section in early November." "VideoLAN, the French nonprofit organization behind the VLC media player, warned that the proposed levy could cost it more than €1 million annually," reports CircleID. "Its response illustrates how traffic-based taxation could affect organizations distributing large volumes of data without corresponding commercial revenue."
