                📅 Oct 31, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

                Destiny 2 sure had a once-in-a-lifetime announcement this year. Three or four of them, in fact. 2026 has been a decade of a year for the game, including death, swan song, glorious rebirth, and an afterlife.

                This week, Bungie detailed all it aims to bring back to the game after being cut in the past years. It’s certainly ambitious, and the studio doesn’t seem too daunted by that prospect—though having the backing of millions of players can’t hurt.

                The return of the missing content by itself isn’t the key takeaway, though. For the first time in years, Bungie’s new leadership seems finally at liberty to communicate openly and sincerely with the Destiny 2 community. No half-concealed words or conveniently ignoring difficult topics, instead embracing the tough questions and finally building momentum.

                Adopting this stance earlier could have meant Destiny 2 wouldn’t need awe-inspiring support from hundreds of thousands of fans to be saved. Maybe it wouldn’t need saving at all.

                It’s refreshing to see the new decision-makers at Bungie being so candid, in particular about hard topics. Of course, saving the game from death through community support earns heaps of goodwill to your fans. But for the first time in a couple of years, the relationship doesn’t feel transactional, dismissive, or outright antagonistic.

                Bungie’s new leadership certainly deserves credit for steering the ship during this comeback. They’re bound to run into some colossal challenges, especially once you look at the extent of everything they plan on reinstating.

                But let’s face it: it wasn’t that hard to do the right thing in the first place.

                I’m not saying this to hate on the new leadership (and I’m using this term broadly to define the people with decision-making power). Head of product Josh Deane, new studio head Poria Torkan, and others have absolutely been doing a great job fostering goodwill, being transparent about its big-picture plans, and sharing timelines, in no small part with the help of community manager Dylan Gafner.

                Because of this new direction, I finally have faith in Bungie for the first time since The Final Shape in mid-2024. Not just because they’re doing the right things, but because, unlike the previous leaders, they’re not doing the wrong things—and for Bungie, that’s often just as important.

                When you look at it, a lot of the studio’s shortcomings were self-inflicted. Siphoning resources from Destiny 2 for an uncertain bet on the nascent Marathon caused a schism that might be irreparable to the community, and the eldest of the two titles undoubtedly suffered for it. The vision for The Edge of Fate seemed borderline sadistic, cranking the power grind back to 11 and branding it as content.

                You might have done too much of this. Image via Bungie

                Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

                Complaints about obvious pain points would go unanswered, particularly after The Edge of Fate. Players were begging for any change, but Bungie’s inaction seemed to show it was unable—or worse, unwilling—to put out fires, instead letting the house burn down. The studio appeared to either not understand or not care about the overwhelming feedback, which feels like a special skill all on its own. It’d clean house at the “worst superpower” contest, that’s for sure.

                Compare it to now. One end-of-service announcement, a killer update, and millions of displays of support later, Deane told Destiny 2 fans not to buy Marathon as a donation to keep the developer afloat because “It’s our job to show up for you.” If I saw a certain CEO writing that a couple of years ago, I would’ve assumed they were either hacked, under duress, or aiming for gold at the World Series of Saying Things They Don’t Mean.

                Fans sent the message loud and clear that the previous approach was unsustainable, which is why Destiny 2 is back from the dead and equipped with new people at the helm. We’ve spent years telling Bungie what not to do, and the new leadership is finally listening and taking it to heart. That’s another skill on its own, of course, especially in a community as varied as Destiny 2‘s.

                Comms are cautious yet candid. The old Bungie might have blurred dates with vague “in a future update,” but the latest announcement is clear: don’t expect the unvaulting until at least early 2028. It’s imperfect and far off and difficult and not what some may have hoped to hear. But it’s real.

                I’m unabashedly excited for new content for Destiny 2 again, which I haven’t been since Heresy. I don’t mind that I’ll have to wait a year and change for it. I know this time, at least it will be done right. There’s also the possible Destiny remaster and whatever’s in the future of the franchise.

                It’s hard not to wonder what would have happened if maybe leadership had changed sooner, before apathy became the norm. It would have been a lot easier to wait two years if the process had started two years ago, so we’d be reaping the benefits of it now—and, as a bonus, we wouldn’t have had to watch Destiny 2 agonize.

                I wish the good news hadn’t come at the cost of the game dying, but I’m glad we’re getting anything, even if it’s a bit far off. Until then, I’m confident Bungie will surprise me along the way, and I don’t even remember the last time I felt that.

                Binance Lost $6.3 Billion to Its Own Signing Machine

                📅 Oct 31, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

                On Thursday evening, 29 October, a Binance hot wallet on Tron sent 612.7 million USDT and 46.4 million TRX to an address the exchange didn't control.

                It took less than two minutes. Ethereum followed. So did Bitcoin, Solana, Optimism, and five other chains. By the time Binance paused withdrawals that night, an attacker had moved roughly $6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes, according to TRM Labs.

                Nothing in crypto's history comes close. The previous record belonged to Bybit for just over 20 months, and the FBI put that theft at $1.5 billion, a little under a quarter of this one.

                "It's the biggest hack in history."

                Aravind Srinivasan, head of the systematic OTC business at market maker GSR, quoted by RTÉ

                The size of the number isn't what kept me reading, though. This line from Binance did: the exchange said it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak." Every one of those transfers was validly signed. Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tron did exactly what they were built to do.

                So how do you lose $6.3 billion without losing a key?

                How an exchange actually holds your coins

                A blockchain accepts any transfer that carries a valid signature for the sending address. It has no way to tell whether that signature came from the rightful owner or from someone who has taken over the process that produces it. Hold on to that point; the whole story turns on it.

                Large exchanges keep most customer assets in cold storage (offline, and slow to move on purpose) and a smaller float in hot wallets, which sign automatically so your withdrawal clears in seconds. "Smaller" is relative. Binance held about $144 billion in custody before the attack, so this loss works out to roughly 4% of it.

                A hot-wallet signer is, by design, an obedient machine. A request comes in, passes a policy check, and gets signed. The key itself sits in a hardware security module (HSM) or a multi-party computation (MPC) setup and never leaves. That keeps the key safe from theft. Whether each incoming request deserves a signature is a separate problem, and a harder one.

                Step one: a DevOps engineer's laptop

                Binance's first explanation was that the incident "may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop," which let the attacker reach an internal service container able to submit withdrawal transactions.

                The story grew the next day. Co-CEO Richard Teng said investigators had found additional intrusion points, that the attacker used a self-destruct mechanism to erase tools and traces, and that Binance is now reviewing endpoints, cloud systems, key management and signing processes across the whole company. It still hasn't said how the laptop was compromised.

                "It involved a more complex attack process."

                Binance co-CEO Richard Teng, in a post on X reported by Forbes

                If that sounds familiar, it should. The Bybit theft also started on a developer's machine: attackers got into Safe{Wallet}'s environment and replaced a JavaScript file so that Bybit's signers approved a transaction they couldn't see clearly. Attackers who target crypto firms have spent years luring crypto developers into fake job interviews whose "coding tests" install malware. Nobody has confirmed that's what happened at Binance. It's the obvious first place to look.

                Step two: fifty signatures and one wallet

                On Ethereum, the attacker used EIP-7702, a feature that went live with the Pectra upgrade on 7 May 2025. It lets an ordinary wallet (an externally owned account, or EOA) point to smart-contract code and run that code as if it were its own. Wallet teams wanted it for batched transactions and sponsored gas fees. Turning it on needs exactly one thing: a signature from the wallet's own key.

                At 20:20:59 UTC, the attacker submitted a single transaction carrying 50 EIP-7702 authorizations, all signed by the hot wallet labeled Binance 14. Each authorization is tied to the account's nonce, a counter that goes up by one with every transaction. A busy exchange wallet's nonce moves constantly, so the attacker prepared 50 consecutive ones; whichever matched at the moment of submission would work. One did.

                That authorization pointed Binance 14 at a sweeper contract that took orders only from the attacker. Three minutes and 24 seconds later, the wallet sent out 167,464 ETH and 63 tokens, including 1.615 billion USDT. The delegation stayed in place afterwards, so customer deposits that kept landing at the same address were swept six more times over the next three and a half hours.

                Two details matter here. “Fifty sequential signatures” means sustained access to the signing path, well beyond one phished approval. And Teng has said the delegation bypassed Binance's usual approval process; the signer produced something its own policy layer never reviewed.

                The technique itself wasn't new. A month after Pectra shipped, Wintermute found that more than 80% of EIP-7702 delegations pointed at copy-pasted sweeper contracts that drain wallets with leaked keys. A December 2025 arXiv paper on EIP-7702 phishing showed that one malicious authorization can hand an attacker persistent control of an account. The Binance attacker ran the same playbook at exchange scale, with Binance's own signer doing the signing.

                Security researcher Taylor Monahan made the key point back in 2025, when those sweeper delegations first spread:

                "It's not actually a 7702 issue."

                Taylor Monahan, speaking to The Block about wallets drained through EIP-7702 (June 2025)

                The feature only does what a valid signature tells it to. The weak point is whoever controls the signing.

                Why "no key leaked" is cold comfort

                TRM's reading of the chain data points the same way. It saw ordinary signed transfers leave Binance wallets on several chains, across different key types, within minutes, and concluded that the attacker could make Binance's hot-wallet signing infrastructure authorize transfers of its choosing.

                That's why Binance's reassurance doesn't reassure me much. If an attacker can submit requests from inside the trusted zone, or quietly edit the checks those requests pass through, the HSM can stay sealed and still sign away the balance. Binance's statement is very likely true. It answers a different question from the one customers are asking. Fireblocks, which builds custody infrastructure, put the practical rule well: treat any signature produced outside your signing platform as an incident.

                The race to freeze the money

                The response was fast, at least for some assets. Within about an hour, Tether had frozen 975.1 million USDT and Circle 823 million USDC in the main receiving wallet, roughly $1.8 billion between them; Circle said it acted in coordination with law enforcement. Tether's total later rose to more than 1.567 billion USDT. Binance now puts everything frozen across issuers and partners at around $3 billion.

                "In coordination with law enforcement, we have frozen more than 800M USDC."

                Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire, posting on X, via Decrypt

                The attacker clearly knew the clock was running. TRM traced about 325 million USDT sold through UniswapX and other intent-based contracts for roughly 122,300 ETH. That implies about $2,650 per ETH at a time when ether traded between $2,300 and $2,350; paying a premium of more than 10% is what urgency looks like on-chain. A second wallet deposited 60 million USDT into Aave and borrowed about 19,760 ETH against it before Aave froze the affected markets. By Bitquery's count, the attacker's ether pile has since grown to 490,361 ETH, mostly from converting stablecoins.

                There's an awkward lesson in that split. The most centralized assets in crypto, dollar stablecoins with an issuer who can blacklist an address, clawed back close to half of the loss within hours. BTC and ETH have nobody to call. Even a freeze isn't the end of it: TRM's Ari Redbord points out that getting frozen funds back requires a separate legal process.

                Who is behind it

                Nobody has been officially named. As of 31 October, no government has publicly attributed the attack, Binance hasn't named a suspect, and its root-cause findings aren't out yet. Analytics firms have shared early assessments based on on-chain patterns; until law enforcement or Binance's post-mortem confirms anything, I'm leaving the question open.

                What the chain data does show is planning. According to TRM, preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft: the attacker's wallets were funded through the Tornado Cash mixer, and transaction signatures were collected in advance. Whoever did this was patient, and had deep access long before the first coin moved.

                What Binance has promised

                Binance says it will cover every loss with company money. It has reserved more than $6.34 billion, about $5 billion of it already held in the same tokens that were taken, and is buying the rest on the market and over the counter. Its emergency SAFU fund alone is worth roughly $1.17 billion.

                Withdrawals are still paused. Binance's 31 October update targets a phased restart within about 34 hours, subject to security checks, and proof-of-reserves results by Monday, 2 November. A technical post-mortem is promised but has no date.

                What has to change

                Bybit's breach began on a developer's machine at a supplier; Binance's began on a DevOps engineer's laptop. Any laptop that can reach production deserves the protection production gets: a dedicated, locked-down device, credentials tied to a hardware key, access that expires when the task is done, and a firm rule against running code from strangers (that recruiter's "take-home assignment" included).

                Binance's signer trusted whatever its internal services handed it. A second approver, running on separate infrastructure that a hijacked container can't touch, should match every large withdrawal to a real customer request before anything is signed. Fireblocks makes a related point: hot-wallet keys should never be usable from a developer machine at all.

                EIP-7702 needs its own rules. A treasury wallet that suddenly delegates to contract code is about as loud a warning as custody gets, and it shows up on-chain for anyone watching. Exchanges should refuse to sign 7702 authorizations unless a human expects one, and a single request for dozens of them, one per upcoming nonce, should page someone immediately.

                Then there's containment. One intruder emptied wallets on ten chains in about 20 minutes, which tells me the signing paths shared far too much. Give each chain and wallet tier its own signer, cap how much value can leave per hour, and halt outflows to unfamiliar addresses automatically. Binance paused withdrawals at about 22:15 UTC, roughly two hours after the first transfers at about 20:05 UTC, and the hijacked Ethereum wallet kept sweeping new deposits even after that.

                If you hold funds on Binance, three things. Expect a wave of "refund" and "compensation" phishing; Binance will never ask for your 2FA codes or recovery phrase. When the proof-of-reserves report lands, use Binance's verification tool to check your balance is included. And once withdrawals reopen, ask yourself whether long-term holdings belong on any exchange at all.

                Four years ago I argued in Regulating Chaos that IoT security would only improve once the law caught up with its weakest devices. Crypto custody has reached the same point, and its weakest device turned out to be a laptop. Monday's reserves report will tell us whether Binance's customers are whole; the post-mortem will tell every other exchange which of its own engineers' desks to check first.

                Disclosure: I hold no position in Binance and have no affiliation with the company.

                The AI-Bubble Scorecard

                📅 Oct 31, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

                As of October 23rd, 2026

                "AI bubble" had one of its loudest weeks of the year. CoreWeave slid to a new 52-week low on financing worries, Nvidia fell 4.4% on October 22, and Ken Griffin told a Citadel conference investors are "almost certainly" in a bubble, which promptly drew pushback from Deutsche Bank's Christian Sewing and BlackRock's Larry Fink. Jensen Huang, meanwhile, said neocloud demand is off the charts, but capital for them is scarce.

                I kept a score of all the pieces I saw this week, so 21 articles, reports, and columns from October 16 to 23 that came up in my searches with enough text to judge. Each piece is scored on its overall verdict: Bubble if it says AI is a bubble and/or about to pop; Not a bubble if it rejects the label or says burst fears are premature; Mixed if it presents both sides or says a bubble exists but isn't about to burst.

                Result: 8 bubble · 4 not a bubble · 9 mixed (21 pieces)

                Oct 16, Open Markets Institute: report on circular financing says the AI bubble is "primed to pop." Bubble

                Oct 16, IoT Analytics: analysis concluding there's no widespread AI bubble. Not a bubble

                Oct 17, Fortune: Wall Street debates whether the warnings are a head fake. Mixed

                Oct 17, The American Bazaar: the bubble "isn't bursting, it's being audited." Mixed

                Oct 18, Bloomberg: billionaires warn of a bubble, Howard Marks unconvinced. Mixed

                Oct 19, CEPR (Dean Baker): AI Bubble Monitor #19 Bubble

                Oct 20, NPR / WBUR: Is the AI boom a bubble waiting to burst? Mixed

                Oct 20, Bloomberg: Griffin says AI is "almost certainly" a bubble. Bubble

                Oct 21, 24/7 Wall St. (via Yahoo Finance): Griffin's bubble remarks. Bubble

                Oct 21, Bloomberg: Federated Hermes CIO says the boom has years to run. Not a bubble

                Oct 21, Bloomberg: Sewing and Fink push back on Griffin. Not a bubble

                Oct 21, Axios: The AI trade gets a reappraisal. Mixed

                Oct 21, Common Dreams: report warns the bubble is "primed to pop." Bubble

                Oct 21, The Blaze: Ed Zitron says the bubble is about to pop. Bubble

                Oct 21, Investing.com: Yardeni says a bubble exists but isn't about to burst. Mixed

                Oct 21, Investing.com: "AI bubble or not," manage the risk. Mixed

                Oct 21, Around Prague: a 16% weekly drop is a correction, not a collapse. Not a bubble

                Oct 22, CounterPunch: is CoreWeave's bad week the beginning of the end? Bubble

                Oct 22, Luminix: the evidence for and against. Mixed

                Oct 23, Asia Times: report says the bubble is "primed to pop." Bubble

                Oct 23, Tech Diplomacy (Substack): boom-or-bubble roundup. Mixed

                Reading the numbers: The bubble narratives are more concentrated than it looks. Three of the eight entries cover the same Open Markets/Americans for Financial Reform report, and two cover the same Griffin remarks, so by distinct underlying argument it's closer to 5 bubble vs 4 not.

                The bigger tell is the mixed column: the most common position this week was some version of Yardeni's line, that the conditions for a bubble are there (its new meter reads 83 out of 100) but the triggers that ended past booms are only partly present (34 out of 100). Almost nobody in the sample argued AI itself is overhyped as a technology; the fight is about debt, financing, and whether the spending pays back in time.

                Google's AI satellite sends a very expensive haiku to Earth

                📅 Oct 31, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

                Google on Friday celebrated receiving a poem from its first experimental orbital AI datacenter satellite.

                The company's Suncatcher satellite, launched at the start of the month and put into low Earth orbit, has responded to a ground station prompt to "Write a haiku from the perspective of a TPU orbiting Earth, with the wonderful world spinning beneath you."

                Travis Beals, senior director of Google's interdisciplinary Paradigms of Intelligence research team, said that with Suncatcher's host and TPU trays powered up and machine learning tests completed, the onboard Gemma 4 model achieved its "Hello World" milestone by sending an inference response from orbit.

                "During a ground-station pass, we uplinked our first prompt to our onboard Gemma 4 open model, asking it to generate a haiku about being in space," wrote Beals in a blog post.

                And as the satellite passed over Svalbard, Norway, the orbiting AI model responded over the downlink:

                Blue marble below,

                Data streams in silent grace,

                Starlight feeds my core. ✨

                Those roughly 20 tokens would cost about $0.000012 if generated through the Google Cloud API, based on Gemma 4 26B's pricing of $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens, excluding input costs.

                Add in a satellite weighing perhaps 500 kg, based on the mass of SpaceX's Starlink satellites, and a retail launch price of around $7,000 per kg, and you have a very expensive haiku.

                According to Google's calculations, if the cost of getting a satellite into low Earth orbit can be brought down to $200/kg, the launch cost amortized over the satellite's useful life (~$810–7,500/kW/year) could be comparable to current electricity spending for terrestrial datacenters in the US (~$570–3,000/kW/year).

                Google predicts that SpaceX could achieve that by 2035, more or less, and considers it strategically beneficial to prototype well in advance of that actually happening.

                After the haiku, Beals said, "we tested space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts reporting the technical status of the payload systems." Next up: tests for evaluating how TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation.

                Google has already done some laboratory testing of its Trillium Cloud TPU and AMD host server to see how well they can withstand a 67 MeV proton beam.

                The system's high-bandwidth memory shows the most sensitivity in terms of the total ionizing dose – it exhibits irregularities after a cumulative dose of 2 krad(Si), which is about 3× Google's minimum requirement for TID survival of 750 rad(Si).

                "For typical transformer workloads, the observed SDC [silent data corruption] rate of approximately one event/17 rad, at an estimated orbital dose of 150 rad(Si)/year, translates to a very low failure probability on the order of 1 per 3 million inferences, assuming 1 inference per second," Google researchers said in a paper published earlier this month.

                "While this error rate is likely acceptable for inference, the impact of SEEs on training jobs, and the efficacy of system-level mitigations, requires further study."

                Indeed, the study will continue. Next year, the plan is to test a pair of interconnected satellites. Rather than lofting large satellites into orbit, Google anticipates sending a constellation of many smaller satellites that communicate with one another. ®

                I Gave My App Away for Free — And It Almost Killed It

                📅 Oct 31, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

                Generosity is a marketing strategy. Unit economics is a survival strategy. Here is how my "Founder's Launch Program" saved my indie app.

                The best week of my indie life.

                It started with a stranger on Reddit.

                He'd tried my native notes app, EpicNotes, on his Xiaomi phone and left a comment: "Feels fast and nice. But there's some minor visual weirdness on my phone." I replied offering him a free 3-month Pro code as a thank-you for the feedback. He said yes. I generated the code in the Play Console, felt like a real company handing out a real perk, and went to sleep happy.

                Then came more. A fellow tester who cancelled his subscription on principle but still sent me bug reports with screenshots. A student from India who emailed: "I'm a student, so I can't afford it. If you could make a lifetime promo code available for me, I would be able to fully use it and provide suggestions and bug reports. Please 🙏"

                I granted him lifetime Pro in about two minutes. It felt amazing. People were using my app. People were talking to me. After six months of building native Kotlin Multiplatform code at night after my day job as a product manager, this was the part that finally felt real.

                I thought I was doing indie development right. I was doing indie development feelingly. Not mathematically.

                The math I refused to do.

                Here's the embarrassing part: I'm a product manager by day. I build business cases for a living. I would never ship a feature at work without a rough cost-benefit estimate.

                And yet at 1 a.m., I was handing out free Pro access to an app with AI features without ever opening a spreadsheet.

                So let me open it now, in public.

                What a free Pro user costs me:

                • Every AI summary and smart web clip is a call to a third-party AI API. Pennies per call — but power users summarize a lot.
                • Every synced note is compute, storage, and bandwidth on my cloud backend.
                • Every 90-day code, and especially every lifetime grant, is a commitment to pay both of those bills for months or years.

                What a free Pro user pays me: $0.

                My actual revenue at the time: three paying subscribers. Single-digit monthly recurring revenue.

                The scary part wasn't that the number was big. It was that the number was small enough to ignore — and big enough to bleed. A leak doesn't need to be a flood to sink a boat that isn't moving.

                Why free users felt like growth (and weren't).

                The indie playbook says: give things away early, collect feedback, build goodwill. And the playbook is right — partially.

                That Xiaomi tester? His free code paid for itself ten times over. He sent screenshots of two real bugs (a settings sheet clipped by system insets, a formatting popup buried under the soft keyboard), his exact device model, and unprompted pricing research: "I have a rule against using subscription-based services." That's the kind of intelligence money can't buy.

                But here's what nobody tells you: most free Pro users don't do that. They redeem the code, run a few AI summaries, and go quiet. No feedback. No review. No referral. Every summary they run is a cost with no return.

                The uncomfortable reframe I had to accept: a free user who costs you money every month is not an asset waiting to convert. It's a liability waiting for your motivation to run out.

                The Pivot: The Founder's Launch Program

                I realized I was trying to force a subscription model on a market that was screaming for a one-time purchase. Multiple users told me, in different words, the same thing: I will not pay monthly.

                So instead of defending my subscription, I stopped fighting subscription fatigue and decided to price for it.

                I just launched the EpicNotes Founder's Launch Program. It is a one-time Lifetime Deal for the first 100 users.

                Here is why I structured it this way:

                1. It solves the subscription fatigue: Users pay once and own the Pro features (including the AI engine) forever. No monthly anxiety.
                2. It solves my unit economics: The upfront cash injection covers my API and server costs for the next year, giving me the runway to keep building without bleeding money every month.
                3. It builds a core community: The 100 "Founders" get direct access to me. Their feedback shapes the roadmap.

                If you are tired of bloated Electron wrappers and want a truly native, privacy-first notes app for Mac and Android, this is your chance to support an indie dev and lock in a lifetime license before the doors close. (Link to the Founder's Launch Program is in my bio/below).

                What I changed (the boring, unsexy fixes).

                1. I hard-paywalled the AI. The free tier now includes the full notes experience — writing, formatting, sync — but zero AI. AI is the only feature with a real marginal cost, so it's the only feature behind the paywall. A free user now costs me roughly the price of storage: pennies.

                2. I put my generosity on a budget. Twenty goodwill codes, total. They now go to people who give something back: detailed feedback, honest reviews, real reach. The tester who sends bug reports with screenshots? Instant yes. A drive-by "send code pls"? A polite no with a link to the free tier.

                3. I asked. I reached out to my core users and told them the truth: solo dev, real server costs, if this app helps you, here's how to keep it alive. Honesty converts better than guilt — and both convert better than silence.

                The Lesson

                Generosity is a marketing strategy. Unit economics is a survival strategy. You need both — but in this order: survive first, then be generous on purpose.

                I'm still giving EpicNotes away to students, testers, and kind strangers on Reddit. I just open the spreadsheet before I open the billing dashboard now.

                If you want to try a native, local-first notes app without the subscription trap, grab a spot in the Founder's Launch Program. Let's build the best productivity tool on the Mac and Android ecosystems together.

                Have you ever been burned by subscription fatigue? Tell me in the comments. And if you want to support an indie dev building native apps, check out EpicNotes below.

                Anthropic takes steps to block Claude from reverse-engineering video games

                📅 Oct 31, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

                According to reporting from Tom's Hardware, Anthropic's Claude AI has quietly started restricting the kinds of work it will do, including modding, decompiling, or reverse-engineering video game code. And though there has as yet been no official announcement about why, the reason is still pretty obvious.  

                The video game community has been in the news a lot lately, first because of the GTA6 leaks that went mega-viral and spurred Take-Two Interactive into getting subpoenas against both Microsoft and Discord in the hopes of finding the responsible parties, and next because the hacking and modding community discovered how much easier AI makes their job.

                SEE ALSO: Claude's new smart reports tell bosses when workers are 'off-topic'

                First, game decompilers went into overdrive, playing around with the source code of multiple different video games to, for example, put Nintendo's Mario inside the dark gothic world of Elden Ring, or import Spider-Man into the Batman: Arkham City game, seamlessly blending the mechanics of one character into the world of another. Next came the ports: World of Warcraft, Call of Duty, and Grand Theft Auto: Vice City made playable in a browser, without the original developers or copyright owners having any say in the matter. 

                These initial modifications and ports were already giving gaming companies nightmares, teasing a future without system gatekeeping, but things really got out of hand with the PlayStation 5 jailbreak, which resulted in everything from backward compatibility with older-gen PlayStation games to cross-platform play, with users figuring out how to run Xbox-exclusive titles like Halo 2 and acclaimed Nintendo titles like Zelda: Breath of the Wild on a jailbroken PS5.

                Given the potential number of lawsuits these jailbreaks could cause, and the astronomically high nature of the monetary damages, it's no surprise that AI companies are scrambling to shut down or severely restrict these pathways, but it's also deeply ironic. As Tom's Hardware reporter Bruno Ferreira notes, this sudden concern for copyright "highlights the irony of frontier AI companies that copied the world's information and art for their training sets and are now concerned with copyright infringement." 

                There's also the ugly truth that, if one company makes a gesture toward respecting copyright law or basic ethics, the bad actors can find another LLM that won't (or hasn't yet) taken the same precautions, creating a kind of AI arms race driven by perverse incentives: the least ethical AI might be poised to become the most popular.
